articles.title: New money, no money, and psychological inheritance in the elasticity of 21st century happiness
articles.authors: Kai Ruggeri; Rafaella Osores Urday; Sofia Pelica; Sarah Ashcroft-Jones
articles.abstract: The role of financial resources in subjective well-being is extensively studied, yet with many unresolved debates on the precise association, inflection points, or applications. Using multidimensional data from 91 countries (N=53,589), we find near-universal support for a positive association, which is strongest in wealthier countries and, globally, highly elastic as household incomes surpass local costs of living. Uniquely, we observe a “psychological inheritance”, where the strongest associations are determined by economic class in childhood, even after significant upward mobility by adulthood. We also find inelasticity in well-being at the top and bottom of income distributions, which largely indicates satiation and decoupling at wealth extremes. Across countries, well-being surpasses average at household incomes around 4.5 times the cost of living. Downward mobility is linked with substantial declines but likewise better outcomes than those of equivalent adult incomes that started lower economically, suggesting a psychological endowment where starting point and relative stability are as vital as growth, though the association is strongest in wealthier countries. The link between income and well-being is therefore strongly supported while personal financial history and broader economic environment have substantial impacts on how money relates to happiness, and thus, to individual and population well-being.

articles.title: Effects of Self- and Other-Referencing Language on Engagement with Science Content on Social Media: A Field Experiment
articles.authors: Zuhe Liu; Joshua L. Schlichting; Lauren K Fink
articles.abstract: The present study tested whether the self-reference effect (SRE)—individuals’ tendency to engage with information related to themselves—can increase engagement with science content on social media. In a 12-week field experiment, we published 34 Instagram posts and 10 YouTube videos featuring a science lab’s activities. Captions and video titles were randomly assigned to either a self-referencing (SR) condition (using second-person pronouns), or an other-referencing (OR) condition (using third-person pronouns). Engagement was assessed using platform metrics such as likes and shares. Contrary to expectations, SR content did not yield higher engagement, whereas OR content yielded significantly higher shares. Exploratory analyses further indicated that OR content yielded higher composite engagement scores. These findings suggest that self-referencing language may have limited effectiveness for science communication in social media settings. Importantly, this study opens avenues for further research on how content framing strategies influences science content engagement on social media.

articles.title: Who Writes the Self? Identity Shift Persists Under AI-Assisted Writing
articles.authors: Zoë Natalia Cullen; Nicole Ellison; Jordyn Young; Andrea Forte
articles.abstract: Identity shift theory holds that selective online self-presentation can shift self-perception toward the portrayed identity, but its mechanisms assume that the presenter wrote the presentation. Generative AI now lets people publish self-presentations they did not fully compose. In a preregistered 2 (extraversion vs. introversion) × 3 (manual writing, AI outline, AI draft) experiment (N = 388), participants assigned to present extraversion rated themselves as more extraverted than those assigned to present introversion (d = 0.32), and the size of this identity shift did not differ across authorship conditions. AI involvement changed the writing process. Participants in both AI conditions searched their memories more deliberately for fitting examples, and participants who edited an AI draft felt less ownership of their text than those who wrote from an AI outline. Neither process accounted for the shift. The presenter need not be the sole author of a self-presentation for it to shape self-perception.

articles.title: When AI becomes social: the promise and risks of AI companions for mental health – a social brain perspective
articles.authors: Benjamin Becker; Nan Qiu; Christian Montag
articles.abstract: AI companions are emerging as psychosocial technologies that may reshape social connection and mental health, while also creating risks of emotional dependence. Here, we propose a social-brain framework explaining how attachment, reward, and emotion regulation systems may shape human–AI bonding. This framework highlights the importance of understanding how AI companionship may reshape social connection and mental health, suggests an overarching model that accounts for the complex interplay between the human interface, technology design and context, and provides insights for the responsible design of future AI systems.

articles.title: Testing different metrics for syntactic and morphological complexity in aphasic discourse: A cross-genre comparison in Spanish
articles.authors: Jorge Ricardo Hidalgo Chagoya; Xabi Ansorena; Roel Jonkers; Maddi Carrera; Ignacio Quemada Ubis; Simona Mancini
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The aim of this study is to determine which of four tasks testing different discourse genres (descriptive, procedural, conversational, and narrative) is the most sensitive in detecting syntactic and morphological complexity deficits in Spanish aphasia. Additionally, we compare two approaches for measuring syntax in discourse to identify the most accurate set of metrics for discriminating group membership.

Method: In this comparative cross-sectional study, we analyzed the discourse of an aphasia group (N = 20) and a non-brain-damaged group (N = 14). Data was preprocessed using manual and automated procedures. We measured syntactic complexity through proxies (mean length of utterance, noun-verb ratio, and verbs per utterance), in addition to a competing ‘syntactic structures’ metric. The latter includes variables of subordination, left branching, relative clauses, and word integration, while morphological complexity was measured through an inflectional index.

Results: The descriptive and narrative tasks highlighted the most significant differences across syntactic complexity metrics between the groups. Additionally, nested binomial logistic regression models showed that the ‘syntactic structures’ metric predicted groups better than the proxies alone.

Conclusions: A comprehensive assessment of syntactic complexity can be obtained through the administration of both descriptive and narrative tasks. The measurement of ‘syntactic structures’ in discourse proved a fitter and more fine-grained approach for group discrimination than the incorporation of syntactic proxies alone. These findings provide guidance for a precise discourse assessment in Spanish aphasia.

articles.title: A Cross-Cultural Comparison of the Attractiveness Halo Effect in Men and Women
articles.authors: Tobias L. Kordsmeyer; Letizia von Dewitz; Yaren Kirma; Sabine Ostermann; Julia Stern; Jean Carlos Natividade; Jaroslava Varella Valentova; Marco Antonio Correa Varella; Lars Penke
articles.abstract: According to the attractiveness halo effect, global person perceptions are biased by physical attractiveness: More attractive people are ascribed positive attributes like competence, prosociality, and health, with cross-cultural variation in such perceptions. However, extant cross-cultural studies mostly considered cross-cultural differences only in either observers or targets. This preregistered study explored cross-cultural nuances in the attractiveness halo effect for Brazilian and German target men and women, as perceived by Brazilian and German observers. Facial photos of 583 targets were judged separately for attractiveness, prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, familiarity, and physical and social dominance by 554 Brazilian and 326 German observers. Ratings between Brazilian and German observers for the same target group and attribute were strongly positively correlated, except for familiarity for German male targets. Attractiveness halo effects were overall strong (stronger for health, social competence, and familiarity compared to social dominance, prosociality, and intelligence) and mostly consistent for Brazilian and German targets and observers, with few exceptions. Only for physical dominance, associations were mixed by target gender and nationality. This study supports a putative universality of attractiveness halo effects and also contributes to a deeper understanding of subtle variations in the halo effects of men’s and women’s attractiveness in more individualistic versus more collectivistic cultures.

articles.title: Affect and Self–Other Risk Judgments: Evidence for Target-Invariant Influence
articles.authors: Erik Hallberg; Pär Bjälkebring; Magnus Bergquist
articles.abstract: Affective evaluations play a central role in risk perception, yet it remains unclear whether affect shapes judgments differently when risks are evaluated for oneself versus others. Across two studies, we tested whether hazard-directed affect exerts a differential influence on self-focused and other-focused risk judgments. Study 1 (N = 77) featured a repeated-measures design in which participants rated affect, perceived risk, and perceived benefit for 13 technologies for themselves and for a random other, allowing within-person comparisons of self- and other-focused judgments. A linear mixed-effects model indicated that although negative affect predicted higher perceived risk and positive affect predicted lower perceived risk, the influence of affect did not differ across judgment targets. With the same design, Study 2 (N = 150) experimentally manipulated hazard-directed affect using negatively versus positively valenced images across five technologies. The positive affect manipulation lowered perceived risk while negative affect increased perceived risk. The influence of the manipulation did not differ across judgment targets. Additionally, we examined whether the inverse association between perceived risk and perceived benefit, an indicator of the affect heuristic, varied by target: evidence for a stronger inverse association for other-focused judgments emerged in Study 1, suggesting affective cues may be relied upon more readily when making judgements for others. This finding did not replicate in Study 2. Together, our findings refine affect-based accounts of risk perception by suggesting affective evaluations of hazards are applied similarly across judgment targets, even when self–other differences in risk level are present.

articles.title: A Relevance Rate Model of the affective mechanisms linking social media use to later attentional disruption
articles.authors: Hippolyte Fournier; eva pool; David Sander; Elise Dan-Glauser
articles.abstract: Social media use is increasingly suspected of harming attention, but the evidence remains too limited to draw any firm conclusions. One obstacle is the lack of a framework specifying how such use might affect attention afterwards, without any device. To address this gap, we draw on emotional attention, the affective mechanism that prioritises what matters to individuals. The Relevance Rate Model rests on the relevance rate, the frequency with which an environment delivers concern-relevant stimuli. Drawing on predictive coding, we suggest that social media raises the rate that users expect, and that this expectation may persist after each session and, with repeated use, across daily life. When an activity delivers less concern-relevant information than expected, sustained attention to the ongoing task may be disrupted as emotional attention is recruited to address the shortfall. The model specifies four measurable parameters of use, from which we derive a research agenda.

articles.title: Etude comparative des répercussions émotionnelles chez les primo-intervenants (pompiers, SMUR) et les psychologues
articles.authors: Violette BARBIER-SORBA; Adolphe Béquet
articles.abstract:
Cette étude s'intéresse aux répercussions émotionnelles liées à la temporalité d’intervention chez deux catégories de professionnels exposées à une forte charge émotionnelle : les primo- intervenants (sapeurs-pompiers, membres du SMUR) et les psychologues, dits « intervenants différés ». L’objectif est de comparer les effets émotionnels selon que l’intervention ait lieu de manière immédiate ou différée. Une étude quantitative a été réalisée auprès de 286 participants âgés de 19 à 67 ans, exerçant comme pompiers, membres du SMUR ou psychologues depuis au moins un an. Ils ont répondu à trois questionnaires : le Work-Related Quality of Life (Van Laar et al., 2007), le Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Watson et al., 1988), et un questionnaire socio-démographique. Les résultats ont permis de montrer qu’aucune différence significative n’a été observée entre primo-intervenants et psychologues concernant les émotions ressenties. En revanche, la qualité de vie au travail est plus élevée chez les psychologues et corrélée à des émotions plus positives. Les analyses statistiques montrent que la qualité de vie et la temporalité d’intervention sont deux prédicteurs significatifs des répercussions émotionnelles, bien qu’insuffisants à les expliquer entièrement. L’analyse lexicale complète ces résultats en mettant en évidence les stratégies de régulation adoptées par les professionnels.
Mots clés : Primo-intervenants, psychologues, traumatisme secondaire, impact émotionnel, qualité de vie au travail

This study focuses on the emotional repercussions related to the timing of intervention among two categories of professionals exposed to high emotional demands: first responders (firefighters, emergency medical service members) and psychologists, referred to as “delayed responders”. The aim is to compare emotional effects depending on whether the intervention occurs immediately or at a later time. A quantitative study was conducted with 286 participants aged 19 to 67, working as firefighters, EMS members, or psychologists for at least one year. They completed three scales : the Work-Related Quality of Life (Van Laar et al., 2007), the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Watson et al., 1988), and a socio-demographic questionnaire. The results showed no significant difference between first responders and psychologists in terms of the emotions experienced. However, psychologists reported a higher quality of work life, which was associated with more positive emotions. Statistical analyses indicate that quality of life and intervention timing are two significant predictors of emotional repercussions, though not sufficient to fully explain them. Lexical analysis complements these findings by highlighting the regulation strategies adopted by professionals.
Keywords: First responders, psychologists, secondary trauma, emotional impact, work-related quality of life.

articles.title: Effects of finding and savoring kawaii aspects of animal pictures on affective ratings, mood, and prosocial behavior
articles.authors: Nonoka Nakamura; Hiroshi Nittono
articles.abstract: The Japanese word ‘kawaii’ describes not only an object’s cute attributes but also a positive feeling toward it. Although viewing cute objects can improve mood and encourage prosocial behavior, it remains unclear whether intentionally focusing on kawaii feelings enhances these effects. In two online experiments, participants viewed pictures of dogs and cats (N = 282) and other animals (N = 435). They were instructed to either find and savor the kawaii aspects of the animals or to find and describe their objective characteristics. The results showed that the picture ratings of valence, arousal, approach motivation, and kawaii were higher in the kawaii condition than in the objective condition. However, no significant differences were found between the conditions in terms of mood change or donation-related voluntary actions. Focusing on kawaii aspects can improve affective evaluation, but a one-time savoring session may not be sufficient to alter mood or behavior.

articles.title: Can AI Scale Human Fact-Checking? Evidence from Community Notes
articles.authors: Thomas Renault; Mohsen Mosleh; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Community Notes---a crowd-based fact-checking program through which social media users can flag a post with a note explaining why the post is misleading, and the note is displayed if a diverse set of users rate the note as helpful---has become central to online content moderation. The program, however, faces substantial scalability constraints, as the generation of notes takes considerable time and effort, and the number of user participants is limited. Here, we investigate whether allowing AI models to write Community Notes helps to alleviate these constraints by analyzing the full corpus of AI-generated Community Notes on X through May 2026. Encouragingly, AI-generated notes are submitted more quickly, are longer, and cite more and higher-quality sources than human-written notes, while being rated helpful at a similar rate and being associated with similar decreases in reposts following the publication of a rated-helpful note. Furthermore, a pre-registered survey experiment finds no statistically detectable difference between AI- and human-generated fact-checks in their effect on belief updating, regardless of whether the author was revealed to participants. On the other hand, AI-generated note writing is highly concentrated, as a handful of accounts produce the large majority of notes, and are significantly less likely to engage with posts involving controversial and polarized topics such as politics and elections. While those findings suggest that AI may be a powerful tool for scaling crowd-based fact-checking systems such as Community Notes, this evolution also entails important risks: shifting the primary bottleneck from note production to note evaluation, moving the system from a decentralized toward a more centralized model, and creating incentives to prioritize claims that are more likely to achieve consensus over those of greater societal importance.

articles.title: Predicting Personality Traits from Short Unstructured Conversations with AI
articles.authors: Daniel Robert Lametti; Ileana Wheeler; Jonah Appleton; Robin Murphy; Santiago Castiello
articles.abstract: Given the complexity of personality, we might assume that significant behaviour is required to express our traits. Here we use large language models (LLMs) to test the extent to which personality is visible in short conversations with artificial intelligence (AI). In a preregistered experiment, 100 participants completed the Big Five Inventory (BFI) before having unstructured conversations with GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words. We then instructed a second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to complete the BFI as if it were each participant, predicting their responses based solely on an analysis of the participant-GPT chats. Correlations between LLM-predicted and self-reported BFI traits were significant (range r = .25 to .47), in some cases matching previously documented self-other predictions from family members. A linguistic analysis revealed that the LLM rater’s predictions relied largely on lexical content as opposed to syntax. Using preexisting data, we tested if the AI’s persona influenced how much participants revealed about themselves in conversation. A hundred participants chatted with two versions of GPT-4.1—one that mirrored their personality (mirror AI) and one that opposed it (inverse AI). The LLM rater predicted BFI traits based on the interactions and we correlated this prediction with self-report. Mirror chats generated significant correlations, averaging r = .41; for inverse chats the average fell to r = .30, and dropped to zero when the prediction relied on lexical content alone. People readily convey their personality profile in short conversations with AI, and this is enhanced when the AI’s persona mirrors the users.

articles.title: Cognitive Model Organism: The Unboxing of Thinking Process
articles.authors: Yuncheng Jia; Bo Qin; Anuchit Phanumartwiwath
articles.abstract: We establish the Hortus Regis Alti (HRA) Experimental and Observational Protocol for studying a frozen language model as a cognitive model organism. The preparation combines controlled input perturbations, complete native-token preservation, deterministic symbolic probes, contextual process coding, and explicit failure screening. One DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B implementation with INT8 linear layers and BF16 elsewhere produced 176 archived trajectories across four observation configurations of one Bayesian decision problem, containing 2,205,963 generated tokens. Eight baseline pairs regenerated identical overlapping prefixes across 93,016 token positions. Three empirical demonstrations organize the study. Symbolic closure separated from execution termination, including renewed processing after a closure marker. Aggregate consumption separated from item-specific response paths: 36 of 40 four-level item series changed direction. Correct local computation separated from maintenance of task representation: an auxiliary result could be calculated correctly and subsequently rebound as an operand. Complete contextual reading localized 1,926 evidence anchors, including successful repairs and recurrent failures. Measurement checks further showed that a short window could classify a long exact cycle as highly diverse. These findings motivate testable hypotheses of representational control competition, training-register capture, and content-specific effects of symbolic continuation. The contribution is a process-oriented experimental preparation, a reproducible trajectory collection, and a quality-control procedure that connects observable symbolic events to discriminating intervention sites. Precision specifications identify the model strain, execution conditions, measurement units, semantic coding decisions, and regeneration range supporting these claims.

articles.title: Human Category Learning in Reversal Tasks: Dynamic Learning Rates Help Overcome Catastrophic Interference in Connectionist Networks
articles.authors: Santiago Castiello; Andrew R Delamater
articles.abstract: During category learning tasks participants often group together, i.e., “commonly code,” within-category exemplars. In two experiments, human participants learned to classify fractal exemplars into two arbitrarily-defined categories. After an initial learning phase, we reversed the exemplar-category assignments in two ways: a Total-Reversal (all assignments were switched) and a Partial-Reversal (only half were switched). If common coding occurs, participants should learn the Total-Reversal faster than the Partial-Reversal and should show within-category interference in the Partial-Reversal task (between reversed and nonreversed exemplars). Our behavioral results supported these predictions and in both experiments we found that participants reach higher accuracy in the Total-Reversal task. To understand the mechanisms behind these findings, we modeled category learning with a 3-layered artificial neural network (ANN). We observed that such models can readily form category representations, but suffer from catastrophic interference during reversal training. To overcome this problem, we modified the networks by applying different dynamic learning rates rules to their different layers. Inspired by associative learning theories (Mackintosh, 1975; Pearce and Hall, 1980), we incorporated a mechanism that promotes slower weight changes in the input-hidden layer and faster changes in the hidden-output layer as the ANN learns the task. This modification allows the ANN in the Total-Reversal task to maintain the category representations in the input-hidden layer simulating our empirical findings. This demonstrates that applying differential dynamic learning rates can help prevent catastrophic interference problems and provide a mechanistic explanation for common coding effects. Our study highlights the importance of associative mechanisms in category learning.

articles.title: Where human similarity holds and where it breaks: Evaluating the alignment of synthetic focus groups
articles.authors: Laura Lara Perez; Paige Evans; Pia Schnabel; Teutly Correia; Joseph Devlin
articles.abstract:
Objective: the growing commercial use of large language model (LLM)-based synthetic participants raises questions about their validity. This study evaluates how reliably text-based synthetic focus groups reproduce human thematic content and interactional dynamics. 

Methods: the assessment used a matched dataset on animal product consumption and gender to generate 30 text-based synthetic focus-group sessions by manipulating agents’ profile levels (basic vs. enriched). Their transcripts were compared with those of five human focus groups using a novel three-level benchmark: thematic fidelity, interaction process, and speaker distinctiveness. 

Results: synthetic groups recovered a plausible subset of human themes but displayed excessive verbosity, internally resolved contrast, less contextually detailed discourse, and reduced speaker distinctiveness. Profile enrichment increased thematic coverage but concentrated discussions around shared ideas. 

Conclusions: these findings position synthetic focus groups as a promising tool for exploratory market research, while underscoring their limitations in capturing situated social interaction. Their suitability depends on the intended use, requiring multi-dimensional validation before application.

articles.title: Understood but Unmoved: A Theory of Trait Judgmentalism and the Architecture of Evaluative Rigidity
articles.authors: Emile Boullineau
articles.abstract:
This paper is the theory-stage statement of the Judgmentalism research programme and the direct companion to a peer-reviewed article now published as Boullineau, E. (2027), Moral violations are made, not found: A theory of motivated violation construction, New Ideas in Psychology, 84, 101313, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.newideapsych.2026.101313. This version supersedes the earlier posted version in full, under a new title, and has been submitted to Review of General Psychology.

Psychology can explain why people condemn, but not who cannot be moved. Everyone knows the evaluator who understands every mitigating fact and remains unmoved. Across moral judgment, person perception and belief updating, paradigms treat comprehension of mitigating context as proof that the context entered the evaluation. Whether it received any weight is a separate question, rarely put. This paper names that default the Revision Assumption and proposes the construct it has hidden. Trait Judgmentalism is a stable individual difference in which an evaluator comprehends relevant, credible mitigation and does not revise the verdict on the person. The mechanism, Contextual Moderation Failure, sits after every input stage has succeeded. The context is perceived, understood, retained and accepted, and it weighs nothing. The trait has an architecture, two candidate antecedents and two expression channels, one of them silent. It is a sibling, not a twin, of dogmatism, of low intellectual humility and of low forgivingness. Five falsifiable predictions follow, and the paper names what would kill the construct. The programme's classification stage is already published. Psychology has measured who judges harshly, who judges at first sight and who judges out loud. It has never measured who cannot be moved. This paper states what it would take.

articles.title: Relational Calibration: A Framework for Dynamic Instructional Regulation in Complex Learning Environments
articles.authors: Delwin B. Carter
articles.abstract: Relational Calibration (RC) is a theoretical framework for organizing enacted instructor responses during ongoing instruction. It specifies three response dimensions: relational positioning, instructional posture, and real-time modulation. Interpersonal attunement coordinates these dimensions by linking emerging instructional evidence and its interpretation to enacted responses. The framework’s functional target is sustaining engagement with demanding intellectual work while preserving intellectual demand. Grounded in research on professional noticing, adaptive and responsive teaching, contingent scaffolding, interpersonal teacher behavior, relational competence, and instructional communication, RC brings relational, instructional, and expressive aspects of response into a common event-level representation. It distinguishes observable evidence, interpretation, enacted response, instructional architecture, the functional target, proposed mechanisms, subsequent outcomes, and measurement. These distinctions provide a basis for examining how instructors coordinate responses within particular instructional events and how those responses relate to engagement and preserved demand. The manuscript develops the framework’s theoretical foundations, dimensions, and coordinating process, then specifies a measurement and research agenda addressing event boundaries, response coding, independent criterion measurement, comparison with established frameworks, and enactment across instructional contexts.

articles.title: Predicting Personality Traits from Short Unstructured Conversations with AI
articles.authors: Daniel Robert Lametti; Ileana Wheeler; Jonah Appleton; Robin Murphy; Santiago Castiello

articles.title: From Behavioral Design to Behavior-Based Design: Functional Specification for Designed Environments
articles.authors: Francesco Di Nocera
articles.abstract: Behavioral design has developed frameworks and taxonomies that help researchers and practitioners organize, select, and describe interventions. However, identifying an intervention technique does not establish the functional relations through which it influences behavior. This article proposes behavior-based design (BBD) as a programmatic approach that places functional specification at the center of the design process. BBD does not introduce new behavioral principles or replace established methods of behavior analysis. Instead, it organizes their application to deliberately designed environments, including digital interfaces, public services, sustainability initiatives, and organizational systems. The article identifies five criteria for adequate functional specification: behavioral precision, functional coherence, discriminability among alternative functional explanations, relevance to design decisions, and empirical accountability. Examples illustrate how the same intervention category may involve different functional relations, leading to different predictions, measurement strategies, and design decisions. Particular attention is given to competing contingencies, maintenance, generalization, and the conditions affecting those responsible for implementing and sustaining interventions. Finally, the article outlines a research agenda for comparing designs informed by explicit functional hypotheses with approaches relying primarily on broader intervention categories. The proposed contribution of BBD is therefore methodological and programmatic: to make functional specification an explicit requirement of design and to evaluate its predictive and practical value through cumulative empirical research.

articles.title: Cognitive Control as a Brake on the Depression–Internet Addiction Link: Task-Based fMRI Evidence from Activation and Task-Modulated Functional Connectivity
articles.authors: JIAJIA ZHU; Tianxiang Jiang; Lawrence Hoc Nang Fong; Anise Wu
articles.abstract: Internet addiction is closely associated with negative emotions such as depression, and cognitive control has been proposed to moderate this relationship. However, the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Using a publicly available fMRI dataset, this study examined whether cognitive control-related brain activation and task-modulated functional connectivity (TMFC) moderate the association between depressive symptoms and Internet addiction. Thirty-four participants completed a global–local attention allocation task during fMRI, the Internet Addiction Test (IAT), and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). Behaviorally, accuracy under conflict conditions negatively moderated the BDI–IAT association. At the neural level, activation in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and left ventromedial prefrontal cortex negatively moderated this association, whereas activation in the right substantia nigra, right nucleus accumbens, and right caudate nucleus positively moderated it. At the network level, stronger functional connectivity between the frontoparietal control network and the subcortical network weakened the positive BDI–IAT association. These findings suggest that prefrontal regions and frontoparietal–subcortical connectivity may buffer the depression–Internet addiction link, whereas subcortical reward- and habit-related regions may amplify it, providing neuroimaging support for the I-PACE model.

articles.title: Toward a Program Theory of A Singaporean Single-Session, Synchronous Chat-Based Mental Health Support for Youths: The Behavior Change Techniques Workers Use and How They Relate to Outcome
articles.authors: Gerard Chung; Lim Tse Min; Joan R. Fang
articles.abstract:
Background: Text-based chat (TBC) services are among the most accessible mental health
support for youth, yet more is known about whether they help than about how they help, that
is, what workers do in sessions. Without an account of these worker skills, TBC services cannot
be reliably trained for or evaluated. This study described the techniques chat workers use,
drawing on the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy (BCTTv1), and linked them to user-
reported outcomes.

Methods: We analyzed 1,439 real chat sessions (44,916 worker turns) from 73 workers at
QuickChat, an anonymous, free, synchronous TBC service for youths aged 12 to 25 in Singapore.
Each worker turn was coded for the presence of 32 behavior change techniques (BCTs). We
examined how often, densely, and broadly techniques were used; how far use varied across
workers; and associations with three post-session outcomes: understanding, coping, and
perspective.

Results: All 32 techniques appeared, but practice was concentrated in a few: social support
(unspecified and emotional), problem solving, re-attribution, and framing/reframing accounted
for over half of all instances. Use varied mainly by session, not by worker, indicating skills
shared across the workforce, not individual styles. Three were positively associated with all
outcomes, namely social support (unspecified and emotional) and information about social and
environmental consequences, though effects were small.

Conclusions: Chat workers deliver change through a small set of core skills, centered on social
support and shared across the workforce. These findings offer a first step toward a program
theory of TBC to guide training and evaluation.

articles.title: Bridging Languages, Rebuilding Communication: Best Practices for Assessing and Treating Discourse for Bilingual People with Aphasia
articles.authors: Danielle Fahey; M K Niharika; Reem S. W. Alyahya; Saryu Sharma
articles.abstract: A considerable proportion of the global adult population is bilingual; however, research on aphasia and language processing remains predominantly centered on monolingual speakers, leading to reduced understanding and guidance about bilingual aphasia. Bilingual aphasia is not equivalent to monolingual aphasia, as bilinguals process each language differently from monolinguals. As such, they are likely to have different error patterns and recovery processes. Best practice for assessing bilingual individuals with aphasia requires evaluating all languages they have sufficiently acquired. Because standardized normative tools are not available for many language combinations or even for numerous individual languages, clinicians can derive necessary insights into a bilingual patient’s linguistic strengths and impairments through systematic discourse sampling. Consequently, we provide best practice recommendations for assessing and treating discourse production in bilingual aphasia. We synthesize current practices in language assessment and treatment of discourse production for bilingual aphasia populations, and provide clinically applicable recommendations for selecting, administering, coding, and interpreting discourse assessments across languages. We also provide recommendations for selecting and adapting discourse interventions, treatment languages, and cross-language targets within the constraints of multilingual clinical service delivery.

articles.title: Toward Sensory Accounts of Autistic Masking: A Perspective
articles.authors: Rebecca Poulsen; Melanie Heyworth; Timothy Chan; Diana Weiting Tan
articles.abstract: Autistic masking has typically been understood as the suppression of natural Autistic traits within neuronormative social contexts. However, social interactions are inherently embedded within broader sensory environments, highlighting the need to consider how sensory experiences shape masking processes. Although sensory experiences have been recognized within existing masking research, the sensory dimensions of masking remain comparatively underexplored. In this perspective, we examine sensory masking as an interrelated dimension of broader Autistic masking processes, defined as the conscious or subconscious suppression, inhibition, or override of sensory responses to meet environmental or social expectations. Drawing on recent research and our own lived experience, we describe how these sensory dimensions may emerge developmentally, often as a learned adaptation to unsafe or invalidating experiences. We then consider the cumulative effects of sustained sensory masking. While sensory masking may serve a functional purpose, its chronic and persistent engagement may contribute to burnout and negatively impact well-being and mental health, particularly in the context of prolonged exposure to sensory aversive environments. We also distinguish these sensory dimensions from related processes of sensory self-regulation and sensory unmasking, which involve supporting regulation and reclaiming autonomy through safe sensory self-expression. We conclude by outlining constructive approaches that support sensory safety, self-regulation, and well-being, and propose future research directions to explore the mechanisms, impacts, and potential supports associated with the sensory dimensions of masking.

articles.title: Postpartum Depression Risk Following Exposure to Universal and Unconditional Perinatal Cash Transfers
articles.authors: Crystal L. Cederna; Rachel Hollander; Jenny LaChance; Sumit Agarwal; Mason Hambley; Eric Finegood; Maya Wolock; Rachel Ablir; Shannon Coughlin; Sooin Choi
articles.abstract:
Purpose. Postpartum depression (PPD) disproportionately affects women experiencing socioeconomic hardship. We examined the association between exposure to Rx Kids, the nation’s first universal and unconditional perinatal cash transfer program, and PPD risk among mothers of one-month-old infants. 

Methods. This study used Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) data collected from electronic health records of 815 one-month well-child visits between 2022 and 2025, spanning two years before and after Rx Kids implementation. Difference-in-differences analyses compared changes in depression screening outcomes among mothers residing in Flint, Michigan, where Rx Kids was implemented, with changes among mothers residing outside Flint. 

Results. In the two years before Rx Kids, the prevalence of high risk PPD scores > 13 was 8.7% in Flint and 6.2% outside Flint; two years after, the prevalence was 3.3% in Flint and 10.4% outside Flint. Rx Kids exposure was associated with a 9.8-percentage-point reduction in high risk PPD scores (95% CI, -16.8 to -2.8, p = 0.006), reversing the preexisting geographic disparity. Reductions were also observed in moderate PPD risk and mean EPDS scores.

Conclusions. Findings suggest that universal and unconditional perinatal cash support may be an effective upstream strategy for preventing PPD, improving maternal mental health, and reducing place-based disparities.

articles.title: Can callous-unemotional (CU) traits be acquired? Tests in a longitudinal sample spanning late childhood through adolescence in the ABCD study
articles.authors: Emily C. Kemp; Meghan Dontha; Zeying Du; Herry Patel; William E. Pelham
articles.abstract: Background. Callous-unemotional (CU) traits (i.e., “Limited Prosocial Emotions”) characterize a particularly severe group of antisocial youth. “Secondary” CU traits, as opposed to “primary,” are distinguished by co-occurring anxiety and are theorized to reflect an acquired phenotype that develops through an interaction between heightened emotional sensitivity and prolonged adversity exposure. The aim of this study was to test this pathway in a large, diverse sample spanning late childhood (age 9-10) to middle adolescence. Methods. Data were drawn from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, with youth (N = 11, 880; Mage = 10; 48% female) assessed annually over five timepoints. Retrospective and prospective analyses examined the effects of emotional sensitivity and different forms of adversity on the development of CU traits. Results. Retrospective analyses showed no main or interactive effects of emotional sensitivity and adversity during late childhood in predicting secondary CU traits by adolescence. Instead, a significant interaction (B = .21, SE = .06, p < .001, RRR = 1.24) was found such that higher overall adversity and emotional sensitivity together increased risk for primary, not secondary, CU traits. Prospective analyses among emotionally sensitive (≥90th percentile) youth with no CU traits (n = 365, age ~10) similarly showed no forms of cumulative adversity predicted increases in or the onset of “elevated” CU traits after four years. Conclusions. Findings did not support a distinct adversity-linked pathway to secondary CU traits via emotional sensitivity. Instead, results were consistent with alternative models in which secondary CU traits reflect a comorbid profile marked by broader clinical severity or overlapping liabilities (e.g., negative affectivity, internalizing risk).

articles.title: The Nature of Phonological Impairments in Dyslexia and Stuttering: Evidence from Phonemic, Semantic, and Design Fluency Tasks
articles.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; James H Smith-Spark; Richard Kirkden
articles.abstract:
Objectives: Using executive fluency tasks, the current study investigated whether these challenges reflect phonological representations themselves or access to intact representations during self-reported adults who stutter (AWS) and self-reported dyslexic adults.
Method: An online, unsupervised sample of 62 self-reported AWS, 62 self-reported dyslexic adults and 62 neurotypical adults completed a modified, typed version of semantic and phonemic fluency, as well as a mouse-drawn version of design fluency. We analyzed switching (shifting between subcategories; proxy for retrieval efficiency) and cluster size (words per subcategory, proxy for representational integrity). 
Results: Controlling for nonverbal IQ and language measures, hierarchical regression showed that dyslexia and stuttering significantly predicted reduced overall phonemic output, whereas semantic and design fluency remained unaffected. Both groups showed reduced switching, though more pronounced in the dyslexia group. Conversely, only stuttering predicted reduced cluster size.
Conclusion: Given the heterogeneity of these neurodivergent profiles, these findings suggest that, in dyslexia, access to phonological representations is affected. Conversely, stuttering affects the representations themselves. For individuals presenting these specific cognitive signatures, interventions could be tailored toward either retrieval strategies or representational strengthening.

articles.title: An Elaborated Model of Youth Externalizing Psychopathology
articles.authors: Irwin Waldman; Holly E Poore
articles.abstract: Externalizing is an integral spectrum in hierarchical dimensional models of psychopathology. Comprehensive models of Externalizing have been developed for late adolescents and adults, but not for youth. We developed and characterized an elaborated model of youth Externalizing psychopathology using item response theory and confirmatory factor analyses of ADHD, ODD, and CD symptoms to investigate the psychometric properties of Externalizing’s components. Participants included large population-representative twin and clinic-referred samples of youth. Using several criteria, increasingly elaborated models comprising an Externalizing dimension and seven fine-grained symptom factors outperformed models containing omnibus ADHD, ODD, and CD symptom dimensions. Results replicated across clinic and twin samples, with the Externalizing dimension most strongly reflecting defiant behavior. Symptom domains varied in their measurement properties across levels of Externalizing. This elaborated model of youth Externalizing sets the stage for future investigations of causes and outcomes, and for examining measurement invariance across individuals of diverse backgrounds.

articles.title: What Makes a Match? Evaluating Visual and Textual Information in Dating Apps' Profiles
articles.authors: Anna Gerna; Marco Marini; Fabio Paglieri; MarcoViola
articles.abstract: Online dating platforms require users to evaluate potential partners based on sparse, highly curated information, typically profile pictures and short self-descriptions. The present study examined how characteristics of visual and textual cues in dating profiles shape overall desirability (i.e., dateability), focusing on physical attractiveness (for photos) or interest (for bios), alongside likability, trustworthiness, and self-confidence. Participants evaluated photos and bios from simulated Tinder profiles, rating these dimensions together with their willingness to date the target. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that, although physical attractiveness and perceived interest were the strongest predictors of willingness to date the target for photos and bios, respectively, other dimensions also played an important role. Crucially, observed associations varied with participants’ gender and prior dating app experience. Gender differences in photo-based evaluations were largely concentrated among experienced users, suggesting that evaluative strategies may differ more with familiarity with dating platforms’ dynamics than by gender alone. Experience was also related to differences in the evaluation of bios, with inexperienced users placing more importance on perceived trustworthiness and self-confidence. Beyond these substantive findings, the study provides an openly available set of ecologically grounded dating-profile stimuli, both visual and textual, empirically characterized across multiple dimensions relevant to social and romantic evaluation. These materials may provide a useful resource for future research on online dating and the integration of visual and textual social information in digital profiles.

articles.title: From Behavioral Instructions to Perceptual Goals: Manipulating Anthropomorphism in Human-AI Communication Experiments
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Researchers commonly manipulate chatbot anthropomorphism through social cues, whose effects vary and may introduce unintended perceptual differences. Generative AI enables an alternative: manipulating perceived characteristics through natural-language prompting. Two online experiments (N = 84 each) evaluated behavior-prescriptive and perception-goal prompting for manipulating anthropomorphism. Study 1 found no significant differences in anthropomorphism. Study 2 found significant differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism (ds = .86–.95), without significant differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence. These findings provide initial empirical support for perception-goal prompting and suggest broader methodological possibilities for manipulating perceived chatbot characteristics in human–AI communication research.

articles_hidden.title: The effectiveness of a therapeutically applied Dungeons and Dragons group intervention in a community mental health setting – Protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
articles_hidden.authors: Terry Rae; Matthew Modini; Poppy Watson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective 
The use of Therapeutically Applied Role-Playing Games (TA-RPGs) in mental health treatment settings has grown in popularity and early efficacy investigations appear promising. However, the use of TA-RPGs for the treatment of anxiety and depression has rarely been studied in people who present with comorbid complex mental health issues. While one recent waitlist-controlled trial has reported that a TA-RPG (Dungeons and Dragons with embedded CBT) reduced mental health symptomatology, this now needs to be replicated with a more robust experimental design. Publishing this protocol methodology before the study is completed aims to increase transparency and aid other researchers conducting similar research in this advancing field.  
Methods 
The authors propose a two-group randomised controlled trial testing the efficacy of a CBT-infused, therapeutically applied, 8-week Dungeons and Dragons group program. An active control group will play board games for a comparable amount of time. Participants will be consumers receiving care at a community mental health centre with complex care needs. Outcome measures for anxiety and depressive symptomatology will be collected before and after participation in both groups, with the intervention group also completing outcome measures at 12 months follow up. In this protocol paper the intervention will be outlined in detail. The trial is registered on the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12625000296437.

articles_hidden.title: New money, no money, and psychological inheritance in the elasticity of 21st century happiness
articles_hidden.authors: Kai Ruggeri; Rafaella Osores Urday; Sofia Pelica; Sarah Ashcroft-Jones
articles_hidden.abstract: The role of financial resources in subjective well-being is extensively studied, yet with many unresolved debates on the precise association, inflection points, or applications. Using multidimensional data from 91 countries (N=53,589), we find near-universal support for a positive association, which is strongest in wealthier countries and, globally, highly elastic as household incomes surpass local costs of living. Uniquely, we observe a “psychological inheritance”, where the strongest associations are determined by economic class in childhood, even after significant upward mobility by adulthood. We also find inelasticity in well-being at the top and bottom of income distributions, which largely indicates satiation and decoupling at wealth extremes. Across countries, well-being surpasses average at household incomes around 4.5 times the cost of living. Downward mobility is linked with substantial declines but likewise better outcomes than those of equivalent adult incomes that started lower economically, suggesting a psychological endowment where starting point and relative stability are as vital as growth, though the association is strongest in wealthier countries. The link between income and well-being is therefore strongly supported while personal financial history and broader economic environment have substantial impacts on how money relates to happiness, and thus, to individual and population well-being.

articles_hidden.title: The Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ):  Measuring Individual Differences in Song Listening
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique T Vuvan; Julia Cannistraro; Rachel Goodkind; Megha Sharda
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent years have seen a significant increase in the use of songs, which contain an integrated music/language signal, as experimental stimuli. This has created a need for standardized tools to measure individual differences in song perception. The current article reports the development of the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), which measures the degree to which a song listener’s cognitive resources are oriented towards the lyrics versus the other musical features (i.e., pitch, rhythm, timbre). In Study 1, we used exploratory factor analysis to reduce 121 candidate items down to 12 items for the LFQ. In Study 2, we used confirmatory factor analysis and internal consistency measures to ascertain the unidimensional structure of the LFQ. In Studies 3 and 4, we demonstrated that the LFQ is correlated to comprehension of lyrics but not to the ability to exactly recall lyrics. In Study 5, we aggregated data from the first four studies to create initial norms for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire and to explore discriminant validity between Lyric Focus and musical and literary activities with more statistical power than in each study alone. The LFQ is presented as a practical, valid, and reliable tool for researchers interested in the relation between music and language.

articles_hidden.title: Overcoming the Empirical Challenges of Geometric Similarities: A Model-Based Review
articles_hidden.authors: Florian Ismael Seitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Similarity is fundamental to cognition, shaping both foundational and higher-order processes. Cognitive theories often adopt a geometric approach, where similarity is defined by the distance or angle between objects in a psychological space, successfully explaining many perceived similarity relations. However, the validity of such geometric similarity models has been questioned by diverse empirical challenges, such as violations of the metric axioms (minimality, symmetry, and triangle inequality), the common features effect (common features increasing similarity), contextual effects (similarity relations shifting with the presence of other objects), and nearest neighbor effects (single objects considered as most similar to many others). The present work reviews evidence showing that geometric similarity models can address many of these challenges through psychologically plausible extensions of the model formalizations. Some extensions add parameters within the standard framework, such as feature-specific attention or object-specific biases (e.g., salience or frequency). Others generalize the geometric framework itself, through similarity functions that go beyond distances or angles, or psychological spaces that represent objects as something other than points on a multidimensional map. Each extension addresses specific empirical challenges while maintaining cognitive plausibility. These findings suggest that geometric models, when appropriately extended, provide a robust foundation for understanding human similarity relations and offer a path toward comprehensive theories of higher-order cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Development and validation of a prognostic tool for antenatal depressive symptoms: Statistical analysis plan for a two-stage model integrating self-reported and biomarker measures
articles_hidden.authors: Ibrahim; Shahirose Sadrudin Premji; Shehzad Ali; Jaime Delgadillo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Antenatal depression is common, under-detected, and harms mothers and infants. Pakistan has Asia’s highest perinatal depression prevalence and an estimated national economic burden of US$16.5 billion. About 9.7 million Pakistani women become pregnant each year, and roughly 3.6 million may experience antenatal depression. Routine detection relies on self-report scales (e.g., Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS]); whether biomarkers add prognostic value is largely untested. 
Objective: Develop and validate a multivariable prognostic tool (MPT) to predict clinically significant depressive symptoms (EPDS ≥ 10) and assess the added value of biomarker data.
Methods: We will use secondary data (N = 1,621) from the Pakistani Pregnancy Cohort at the Aga Khan Hospital for Women and Children, Sindh. Self-reported predictors across eight domains (demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, mental health, clinical history, pregnancy-related, and social network) plus biomarkers will inform MPT development. In Stage 1 we will compare supervised classifiers (regularized regression, decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks) to logistic regression. Models will be trained with stratified five-fold cross-validation and nested L1 selection within folds to retain the smallest predictor set within 0.01 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of the full mode. External cross-validation on an independent hold-out sample will report ROC-AUC, area under the precision-recall curve (relative to prevalence), calibration, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. Decision thresholds will be set on training data and applied unchanged. In Stage 2 we will build a biomarker-augmented model and compare it to the optimized self-report model using paired AUC tests and reclassification metrics; exploratory clustering will identify participant subgroups. Pre-specified criteria (ROC-AUC ≥ 0.70; calibration slope 0.8–1.2; sensitivity ≥ 0.70; positive net benefit) will determine progression to prospective validation studies in new samples. 
Expected Outcomes: A pragmatic self-report prognostic tool and evidence on whether biomarkers meaningfully improve prediction and justify added complexity.

articles_hidden.title: Characterizing the Association between Delinquency and Parenting Practices Across Adolescence: Longitudinal Associations and the Role of Genetic Liability
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah J Brislin; Maia Choi; Leigh Lustig; Holly E Poore; Sally I Kuo; Danielle Dick
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Parenting practices are a potential mechanism through which adolescent delinquent behavior can be modified. However, it remains unclear whether associations between parenting and delinquency reflect stable differences between families or dynamic processes unfolding within families over time. The current study disentangled the between- and within-person associations between delinquency and parenting across adolescence and whether genetic propensity toward externalizing, indexed by a polygenic score (EXT PGS), was associated with stable between-person differences in delinquency and parenting 

Methods: Participants were 2,184 adolescents assessed annually from ages 12 to 17 as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development- Social Development sub-study. Parents and youth reported on delinquency and parenting dimensions (corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, poor monitoring, positive parenting). Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models separated between-person and within-person associations. We evaluated the association between the EXT PGS and the random intercepts. 
Results: Between-persons, adolescents with higher average delinquency experienced higher average levels of corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring and lower positive parenting. EXT PGS was associated with higher levels of delinquency and with higher corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring, as well as lower youth-reported positive parenting and accounted for approximately 4%–8% of variance shared between delinquency and parenting. Within-person, higher delinquency was associated with subsequent increases in youth-reported corporal punishment, but not parent-reported corporal punishment. Reciprocal associations emerged between delinquency and poor monitoring in both parent- and youth-report models and between delinquency and youth-reported inconsistent discipline. No longitudinal associations emerged between positive parenting and delinquency.
Conclusions: Associations between parenting and delinquency reflected both stable individual differences and dynamic developmental processes. The EXT PGS contributed to stable differences in delinquency and parenting, while longitudinal associations varied across parenting dimensions. These findings suggest that a focus on decreasing inconsistent discipline and increasing parental monitoring may be particularly relevant for mitigating delinquency.

articles_hidden.title: Polarity and the speed of scalar implicature processing
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Vrazitulis; J E Loy; Vera Demberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Scalar implicatures (SIs) such as the inference from 'some' to 'some but not all' are known to vary in processing cost. According to the Polarity Hypothesis (van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021), this cost depends on the polarity of the scalar term: SIs from positively polar expressions (e.g., 'some' implicating 'some but not all') are expected to be slower to compute than literal interpretations, while the reverse should hold for SIs from negatively polar expressions, sometimes referred to as indirect SIs (e.g., 'not all' implicating 'not all but some'). We tested this prediction in a sentence–picture verification experiment with 538 English-speaking participants. Each participant judged whether sentences containing weak or strong scalar terms matched a corresponding picture, allowing us to measure response times as an index of processing effort. Our results showed no clear evidence for the Polarity Hypothesis effect. Specifically, we found that the effect strongly varies across the different scales included in our experiment. We additionally conducted a meta-analysis pooling our estimate with all existing evidence so far: the pooled effect is small and in the predicted direction, but the study-specific estimates behind it vary widely in magnitude. Surprisingly, our results do also not clearly validate the traditional assumption of a B&N effect (Bott & Noveck, 2004), i.e., a general polarity-independent processing slowdown under SIs: a subsequent analysis including trial order revealed that the B&N effect was present in early trials of our study, whereas later trials do not show the effect. Overall, we conclude that polarity may influence the speed of scalar implicature processing, but that this effect is not robust across all types of scales.

articles_hidden.title: A partial least squares approach for within-subject correlations in neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Isaac Kinley; Reece Pierre Roberts; Donna Rose Addis
articles_hidden.abstract: Partial least squares correlation (PLSC) is a multivariate technique used in neuroscience to capture patterns of relationships between neural data and covariates of interest. Conventionally, PLSC captures between-subjects correlations (e.g., between average neural activation and average task performance). However, within-subject correlations (e.g., trial-by-trial relationships between neural activation and subjective ratings or stimulus attributes) are often of interest as well. Thus, we introduce an extension of PLSC to capture within-subject correlations. We validate this approach against related parametric methods and demonstrate that it detects known effects in simulated data and reproduces published findings in open fMRI and EEG datasets. This method is freely available as part of the pyplsc and mne-plsc Python packages.

articles_hidden.title: The Cognitive Structure of the WPPSI-IV: What Can Network Analysis Tell Us?
articles_hidden.authors: John Hite
articles_hidden.abstract: The Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition (WPPSI-IV), is widely used to assess young children’s cognitive abilities. Its indices describe performance in domains such as verbal comprehension and working memory, but evidence for interpreting these as distinct abilities remains limited. This study examined whether exploratory graph analysis (EGA), a network method, could recover the proposed index groupings from published normative correlations for ages 2:6 to 3:11 (n = 600) and 4:0 to 7:7 (n = 1,100). Simulations tested whether the same method could recover those groupings when separate, correlated factors generated the data. The main EGA procedure placed the primary subtests in one group. It also produced one group in 99.6% to 100% of samples generated from the index models, so it could not distinguish those models from simpler alternatives. In the older band, however, factor models fit better with several factors than with one. Recovery depended on factor correlations, the number of subtests per factor, and a built-in check for a single dimension. Groupings also changed with subtest coverage. For school psychologists, a one-group network result, however consistent, cannot by itself show whether WPPSI-IV index scores reflect distinct abilities.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond individual features: Identifying computational principles in perceiving visual beauty
articles_hidden.authors: Mustafa Alperen Ekinci; Philipp Flieger; Daniel Kaiser
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research in empirical aesthetics has related beauty to visual features like curvature, color, or shape. Although these feature-based accounts have identified reliable visual correlates of beauty, the literature on feature preferences is highly fragmented, with individual features studied for individual stimulus domains. Here, we argue that making further progress hinges on complementing feature-based approaches with approaches aimed at distilling computational principles that underlie the perception of beauty. Recent advances in computational neuroscience can drive this new line of research by linking visual beauty to the coding of visual information in artificial neural networks and the biological brain. We highlight two examples of how this approach has identified overarching computational principles. First, metabolic processing costs, both in artificial and biological vision, are inversely related to perceived beauty, suggesting that beauty may reflect energy-efficient, fluent visual coding. Second, integrative processing in artificial and biological vision captures the efficient spatial representation of image elements across space and predicts beauty ratings. Synthesizing these findings, we derive a neuro-computational framework for assessing computational principles in the perception of beauty, which uses artificial neural networks for exploration at scale and then validates candidate principles using human behavior and brain data. We discuss candidate principles that could be explored using this approach, like spatiotemporal predictability, and delineate how the new insights could be reconciled with feature-based approaches. In conclusion, complementing feature-based studies with studies targeting computational principles promises a comprehensive and mechanistic understanding of why certain visual stimuli are perceived as beautiful, and others are not.

articles_hidden.title: Collider Bias in Partner Preference Research: A Methodological Extension of Eastwick et al. (2024)
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Lange
articles_hidden.abstract: Observational research on partner preference-matching commonly conditions on a sample of (most desired) partners. When examined through the lens of causal inference, this configuration constitutes conditioning on a collider variable. This thesis introduces and applies directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) as a framework for assessing corresponding collider bias within the large-scale cross-cultural dataset of Eastwick et al. (2024, N = 10,358, 43 countries). Building on this, a three-layer methodological framework is developed to distinguish three distinct sources of bias: confounding by measured background characteristics, intertrait confounding among the 35 attributes, and residual collider restriction bias arising from the sampling procedure itself. The trait-by-trait level metric of Eastwick et al. (2024) was replicated, followed by a hierarchical multivariate extension entering all 35 ideal preferences and partner attributes simultaneously across four nested models. Results show that demographic and individual-difference covariates contribute low aggregate variance (H1), that multivariate adjustment substantially attenuates both main effects and preference-matching interactions relative to the trait-by-trait approach (H2), and that idiosyncratic matching effects remain near zero even after full adjustment (H3). The discussion situates these findings within the broader context of the research design. Taken together, the methodological evaluation raises the question whether the original preference-matching hypothesis (H0) is adequately testable under the conditions of the present study design. The conclusion identifies the analysis of unselected peer targets as the most direct empirical path toward disentangling residual collider bias from genuine absence of idiosyncratic matching.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Symptoms Interactions Fail to Predict Future Symptom States Across Four Ecological Momentary Assessment Datasets
articles_hidden.authors: Leema Hamid; Sílvia García-Hernández; Björn S. Siepe; Marius Gruber; Jonathan Repple; Andreas Reif; Manuel Brenner
articles_hidden.abstract: Symptom networks have emerged as a popular framework for characterizing the interactions among psychiatric symptoms. Estimated from longitudinal ecological momentary assessment (EMA) recordings, they promise individualized insights into psychopathology and its treatment. Yet whether these networks can be robustly estimated from the short, noisy, and irregularly sampled time series typical of EMA studies remains an open question. We address this through the lens of predictive validity: do estimated cross-symptom connections improve forecasts of future symptom states? In a systematic analysis spanning four public EMA datasets covering different symptoms and sampling schemes, we find that they largely do not. In 273 of 313 participants, symptom networks are outperformed by networks that only use every individual symptom's past to predict its future, indicating that estimated cross-symptom connections tend to worsen out-of-sample predictions rather than improve them. This pattern holds across estimation strategies from unregularized Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to multilevel hierarchical modeling and nonlinear state-space models, suggesting that cross-symptom connections are difficult to identify given the characteristics of real EMA data. Simulation studies support this interpretation, showing that even when ground-truth data is generated by a network model mirroring realistic EMA conditions, cross-symptom structure is often not recovered with sufficient precision to yield a predictive advantage. These findings raise questions about the interpretive framework built on idiographic symptom networks, and suggest that progress may require either measurement designs that make cross-symptom influence more identifiable, or models with less ambitious inferential targets than the recovery of directed cross-symptom effects.

articles_hidden.title: Refining MLU-like metrics in parent-child speech: Measurement properties and decision aids for language-inclusive measures of speech complexity
articles_hidden.authors: Rui Qi Choo; Yi Han Victoria Chua; Fei Ting Woon; Annabel Loh; Shaza binte Amran; Vinitha Selvarajan; Sheetal Sahana Vimalraj; Wong Jin Yi; Suzy J Styles
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mean Length Utterance (MLU) has two problems: High analytic flexibility, and a lack of theoretical justification for data handling choices (e.g., selection of metrics; approach to multilingual speech). We evaluate multiple MLU-like metrics in a large corpus of child-directed speech from multilingual Singapore. Using an existing dataset of wordless picture-book sharing between parent-child dyads with frequent translanguaging (N = 146: English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay, Tamil), we compare metrics across the full sample, and common subsamples. 
Total speech, central tendency and extreme bounds of complexity all show significant developmental trajectories (p<.05), with larger effect sizes when larger subsamples are included in analysis. The metrics perform well when samples are maximally inclusive for languages spoken and types of speech. As some metrics performed better in certain contexts, we present a decision-tree as a reproducible, pre-registerable pathway for deciding which measurement of MLU-like syntactic complexity is best for data of different types.

articles_hidden.title: The FlexER-Scale: A new Self-report Measure of Individual Differences in Emotion Regulation Flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Anne Gärtner; Christoph Scheffel; Timo Schweikert; Denise Dörfel
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous research on emotion regulation (ER) has primarily focused on individual strategies and their association with well-being and psychopathology. Recent frameworks emphasize a context-sensitive, goal-dependent approach, defining ER flexibility as the ability to adaptively adjust ER strategies based on contextual demands and personal goals. Despite growing evidence for its relevance, a concise self-report measure designed to capture trait-level, strategy-independent ER flexibility has been lacking. To address this gap, we developed the Flexible Emotion Regulation Scale (FlexER-Scale) and validated it using data from four independent samples (N = 1,019). Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in an independent sample examined the scale’s structure; criterion validity was assessed via correlations with the WHO-5 Well-Being Index and the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ). The final 10-item FlexER-Scale demonstrated good psychometric properties, including satisfactory item discrimination and high internal consistency (α = .85). EFA suggested a two-factor structure differentiating hedonic and contra-hedonic ER flexibility, which was supported by CFA. The FlexER-Scale showed a significant positive correlation with psychological well-being, driven by the hedonic factor. Small but significant correlations with habitual reappraisal and suppression use provided initial evidence for discriminant validity. The FlexER-Scale is a promising tool for assessing ER flexibility, offering a concise alternative to existing measures by capturing adaptive regulatory variability without relying on predefined strategies. Future research should examine its construct validity, longitudinal stability, and predictive validity. Given that the validation was based on predominantly student samples from a German-speaking context, broader generalizability remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Large Eating Episodes, Cannabis Use, and Health in US Adults: A Cross-Sectional and Exploratory Mortality Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Kavish Chapra; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles_hidden.abstract: Cannabis use is common and increases appetite, which may lead to large eating episodes that overlap with binge eating pathology. However, whether large eating episodes are related to health outcomes among individuals who use cannabis is not known. To address this gap, we analyzed seven cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES; 2005 to 2018) including 18,709 adults aged 20 to 59 years (2,578 current, 7,394 past, and 8,737 never cannabis users). A large eating episode was defined as an eating occasion of at least 1,500 kcal on either of two 24-hour dietary recalls. Among current cannabis users, survey-weighted logistic regression with Benjamini-Hochberg correction estimated adjusted associations between large eating episodes and 29 health outcomes. The weighted prevalence of a large eating episode was 30.3% among current cannabis users, 22.2% among past users, and 19.3% among never users. Among current users, a large eating episode was associated with higher odds of fair or poor self-rated health (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 1.75, 95% CI [1.27, 2.41], p < .001, q = .022). No other association remained significant after correction, although nominal associations were observed for household food insecurity, obesity, abdominal obesity, and elevated glycated hemoglobin. Notably, adults with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode had higher odds of fair or poor health than each of the other three groups (ORs = 1.79 to 1.85, all p < .001). In exploratory analyses, the hazard of death was higher for adults with both exposures after adjustment for age and sex (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.08, 95% CI [1.31, 3.31]), though it did not remain significantly higher after full adjustment (HR = 1.40, 95% CI [0.88, 2.21]). Findings suggest that asking about eating patterns may help clinicians identify individuals who use cannabis and may be experiencing health-related distress. Longitudinal studies measuring loss of control over eating, cannabis frequency, and product type are critical for determining whether eating patterns affect health.

articles_hidden.title: Prevalence, Burden, and Disability Associated with Co-occurring Binge Eating Among U.S. Adults with Cannabis-Involved Drug Use Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Ya-Wen Chang; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite established appetite-stimulating effects of cannabis use, binge eating is seldom assessed in these samples. Its prevalence, clinical importance, and demographic reach among people with cannabis-involved drug use disorder are largely unknown. We analyzed 12,591 adults from the Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys who completed the eating disorder and substance use modules. Using design-weighted estimation, we estimated prevalence of binge eating among adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder and examined whether binge eating marks greater burden and disability and whether it differs by demographic group. Recurrent binge eating affected 11.2% of adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder (95% CI [8.4, 14.7]). Separately, 5.5% met criteria for DSM-IV binge eating disorder. Prevalence rose across levels of cannabis involvement (adjusted OR per level = 2.11, 95% CI [1.75, 2.55]). Adults with both conditions had the highest prevalence of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, major depression, and generalized anxiety disorder. At least one lifetime suicide attempt was reported by 27.8% of this group and by only 3.3% of adults with neither condition. Binge eating alone was associated with a level of functional disability comparable to cannabis-involved drug use disorder alone, while adults with both conditions had the highest WHODAS time out of role and role impairment scores. Among adults with cannabis-involved drug use disorder, binge eating also marked a more damaging drug course. Among adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder, recurrent binge eating was more prevalent among women (17.4%) than men (8.6%). Men nevertheless made up an estimated 54.1% of affected adults. Prevalence ranged from 9.7% to 12.3% across racial and ethnic groups. Findings indicate that binge eating is common and linked with adverse outcomes among those with cannabis-involved drug use disorder, thus warranting targeted interventions.

articles_hidden.title: How Asian American and Black American Adults Define Ethnicity, Race, and Nationality: A Qualitative Thematic Analysis
