articles_hidden.authors: Shujianing Li; Daniel James Sanji; Richard M. Lee; Sa-kiera Tiarra Jolynn Hudson
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on ethnicity, race, and nationality often conceptualizes and measures these identities independently, overlooking their interconnectedness. Perceptions of, and associations among, these identities could differ across racial groups, given distinct migration and racialization contexts in the U.S. Furthermore, nationality has not been thoroughly explored in ethnicity and race research. This study examined how individuals from groups with different migration and racialization histories (i.e., Asian and Black Americans) define ethnicity, race, and nationality. In a cross-sectional survey conducted on Prolific, 299 Asian American and 284 Black American adult participants reported their definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality using open-ended responses. The definitions were thematically analyzed and reviewed between- and within-group variations. Definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality shared similarities between samples: ethnicity by cultural components or family and ancestry; race by shared physical, genetic, and biological traits; and nationality by birthplace, belonging, and affiliation. Geographic locations also defined all three identities. However, Asian Americans commonly perceived ethnicity as narrower than race. Black Americans viewed the two identities as interchangeable and more frequently defined race as a social construct. Nationality had more ties to citizenship for Asian Americans than for Black Americans. Improved theorization and measurement of ethnic, racial, and national identity and the explicit inclusion of national contexts when discussing ethnic-racial identities are necessary.

articles_hidden.title: Neural correlates of dreaming during N2 sleep: Spatial and phenomenological characteristics
articles_hidden.authors: Vincent Rochas; Kevin Mammeri; Laurence Bayer; Giulio Tononi; Lampros Perogamvros
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous studies on the neural correlates of dreaming using high-density EEG (hdEEG) and the serial awakening paradigm have identified posterior brain regions related to dreaming, with maximal activity over occipital areas. Here, we first aimed to extend these findings by examining EEG activity associated with dreaming during N2 sleep in a larger sample and using improved analytical methods. Second, we investigated whether EEG activity was associated with continuous ratings of perceptual and thought-related experiences. We have applied hdEEG (256 electrodes) with source localization and the serial awakening paradigm in N2 sleep of 39 participants to study the neural activity during different time windows preceding each awakening. We found that having a conscious experience with recall (CE) compared to no experience (NE) is related to increased beta/gamma frequencies in a widely distributed part of the cortex, with peak T-values in posterior occipital-temporal regions in the longer time window (30 s), and in parietal regions in the shorter time window (20 s). Exploratory regression analyses revealed significant associations between EEG activity and thought-related experience, but not perceptual experience. These findings highlight the need to distinguish between the neural correlates of different dimensions of dream experience and to investigate their temporal characteristics and variations across sleep stages.

articles_hidden.title: Bringing developmental science closer to families: Caregivers’ and professionals’ perspectives on participation in early childhood research
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Maria Portugal; Eugénia Ribeiro; Marlene Sousa; Isabel Soares; Adriana Sampaio
articles_hidden.abstract:
Developmental research has historically underrepresented families experiencing psychosocial adversity, partly due to barriers posed by in-person laboratory paradigms. Online, webcam-based methods may support more inclusive research, but their design must be informed by the communities they seek to include.
Four focus groups were conducted with caregivers of young children (n = 10) and professionals from child protection, health, and education settings (n = 12), exploring barriers and facilitators to participation, and attitudes toward online data collection. Transcripts were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with participant resonance checks.
Families expressed concerns about privacy and the use of children’s images, while professionals described hypervigilance towards authority among multi-challenged families. Developmental feedback and resources were valued over financial incentives, and online participation was viewed favourably, conditional on material and researcher support. Inclusive developmental science requires moving closer to families’ spaces and priorities, for instance by running studies in places families already use.

articles_hidden.title: Linking Error Estimation for Mean-Geometric Mean and Pairwise Haberman Linking Across Multiple Time Points in the 2PL Model
articles_hidden.authors: Oskar Engels; Oliver Lüdtke; Alexander Robitzsch
articles_hidden.abstract: Longitudinal assessments link test forms through common items. Under item parameter drift, linked ability means and standard deviations depend on the item selection, adding a linking error (LE) to the standard error (SE). Treating mean-geometric mean linking and pairwise Haberman linking across three time points in the two-parameter logistic model as M-estimators, this article derives closed-form LEs and sandwich estimators of LE, SE, and total error (TE). Sandwich and item jackknife LE estimators are bias-corrected for person sampling, including dependent samples. In a simulation study, SE-based intervals undercovered increasingly with sample size, bias-corrected jackknife TE intervals reached acceptable coverage almost everywhere, and sandwich-based intervals undercovered with few items. Longitudinal mathematics data illustrate the estimators, with the LE exceeding the SE.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptive auditory stimulation sustains auditory-respiratory coordination and promotes slowing of spontaneous breathing
articles_hidden.authors: Bavo Van Kerrebroeck; Pieter-Jan Maes; Ilse Van Diest
articles_hidden.abstract: Auditory feedback may influence breathing without explicit instructions to regulate it, but its precise impact remains unclear. We examined responses to adaptive and nonadaptive breath-like sounds during passive listening. Thirty-nine young adults completed four counterbalanced conditions: nonrhythmic filtered noise (Static), rhythmic sounds progressively slowing or speeding relative to initial breathing rate (Slowing and Speeding respectively), and sound adapting continuously to respiratory frequency and phase with a prescribed phase delay relative to respiration (Adaptive). Each condition included 4 min of nominal silence followed by 4 min of stimulation. Primary outcomes were breathing rate slopes, auditory–respiratory phase locking as a measure of auditory-respiratory coordination, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and subjective relaxation. Breathing-rate trajectories differed across conditions; Adaptive showed a more negative slope than Static, although average rates were similar. Phase locking was higher and more sustained during Adaptive than during the nonadaptive rhythmic conditions. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia trajectories differed, but planned contrasts did not survive multiplicity correction. A relaxation composite score did not differ by condition, but an item-level analysis indicated less physical relaxation after Adaptive than Static. Secondary outcomes provided no evidence of increased cardiorespiratory coupling or reduced upper-trapezius muscle activity. Interestingly, the negative breathing-rate trajectories remained significantly different in Adaptive compared to Static after retaining only the 25 respondents that did not notice the sound’s adaptation to their breathing. These findings support adaptive auditory stimulation as a means of supporting auditory-respiratory coordination during uninstructed listening, with a modest and relative change in breathing rate. Clinical benefits and independence from intentional breathing control remain to be tested.

articles_hidden.title: Trust in AI: A Decision-Theoretic framework for Human–AI Interactions in the Digital Society
articles_hidden.authors: Leendert van Maanen; Martijn Mulder; Baptist Liefooghe
articles_hidden.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is crucial for ensuring productive human–AI interactions across domains ranging from medicine to finance. As AI systems become central in the digital society, understanding how people decide when to rely on algorithmic advice becomes increasingly important. This paper proposes that a decision-theoretic perspective is needed to explain how well-calibrated trust in AI can be achieved. We conceptualize trust in AI as a decision to delegate control to an artificial agent, balancing potential rewards and risks of following AI advice versus relying on one’s own judgment. Framed this way, established decision-making theories such as Prospect Theory, Evidence Accumulation Models, and Reinforcement Learning offer valuable insights into the cognitive processes that underlie trust in AI. These theories offer formal, computational models to explain how individuals evaluate AI-generated advice, weigh risks and rewards, form biases, and update trust based on feedback, enabling precise hypotheses about when and why people accept or reject AI advice. By grounding trust in cognitive theory, we offer a roadmap for empirical research that moves beyond surface-level behaviors and toward mechanistic understanding. We conclude that a decision-theoretic approach can enhance psychological insight and guide the responsible design of AI systems within the digital society that are better aligned with human cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Early-life adversity, childhood loneliness, and young adulthood educational achievement: a prospective study
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Cachón-Alonso; Sari Mullola; Jeanne Brooks-Gunn; Christian Hakulinen; Kaisla Komulainen; Marko Elovainio
articles_hidden.abstract: We examine (1) whether indicators of early-life adversity are associated with children’s loneliness complaints and their recurrence at ages 5 and 9; and (2) whether children’s loneliness complaints are associated with poorer educational achievement measured at age 22 after adjusting for early-life adversity indicators. We used data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (US, original sample n=4,898; study sample n=2,456). Children’s loneliness complaints were reported by the principal caregiver. We applied (1) binomial logistic regression and (2) weighted g-computation. In our sample, 6.8% of children had recurrent caregiver-reported loneliness complaints. Indicators of socioenvironmental early-life adversity were associated with higher odds of loneliness complaints. Moreover, higher material hardship and lower neighborhood collective efficacy were associated with higher odds of complaints recurring at ages 5 and 9. We observed no association between caregiver-reported loneliness in childhood and later educational achievement. We note limitations in our measurement of childhood loneliness.

articles_hidden.title: Visual Properties of E-Mobility Devices Shape Their On-Road Vulnerability: Effects of Size and Speed
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Wang; Madeline Jarvis; Ella Du Plessis; Ariella Stephen; Blake Jones; Narelle Haworth; Hinze Hogendoorn
articles_hidden.abstract: The brief visual window—often only hundreds of milliseconds—in which drivers predict the arrival of oncoming vehicles and decide whether to give way is critical for safe and efficient manoeuvring. E-mobility devices (EMDs) are a relatively new form of transportation and may challenge these decisions due to their small visual profile and relatively high operating speeds. Here, we examined whether observers show systematic biases when judging EMDs relative to other common vehicles, potentially contributing to their vulnerability in intersection crashes. Using naturalistic video stimuli spanning seven vehicle categories, we tested whether observers would overestimate the time-to-arrival (TTA) of EMDs and, consequently, accept smaller gaps for them to pass through an intersection. Consistent with this prediction, EMDs elicited greater biases in both TTA and gap judgements (N = 31 and N = 59), with these effects further amplified on a visually complex road. By comparing across vehicle categories under naturalistic viewing conditions, the results provide evidence that the amplified biases observed for EMDs arise from differences in the underlying visual signals available to observers—specifically, their smaller retinal size and potentially less reliable motion cues at higher speeds. Importantly, these biases were not explained by speed misperception: in a separate two-alternative forced-choice task (N = 49), EMDs were perceived as faster, not slower, than other vehicles at matched speeds. This dissociation indicates that TTA overestimation cannot be attributed to speed underestimation alone. Together, these findings link controlled psychophysical processes to real-world traffic behaviour, with implications for future experimental design and traffic safety policy.

articles_hidden.title: The Benefits of and Motivations Behind Large-Team Coordination in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Sajedeh Rasti; Krist Vaesen; Daniel Lakens
articles_hidden.abstract: To increase coordination in science in areas where this would be beneficial for knowledge generation, collaborative work needs to offer clear benefits to individual researchers. This study investigates the motivations for initiating large-team papers and the potential benefits of these projects in psychology. By qualitatively analyzing 500 papers, we find that large-team collaborations are most often instigated to deal with the practical challenges  inherent to complex research questions, but can also be motivated by broader social and or strategic factors. The results from quantitatively analyzing 1,699,513 papers published between 1975 and 2024 indicate that large-team collaborations are more likely to be cited and to appear in higher-ranked journals. Furthermore, their immediate impact on the field, as measured by citation counts within the first 2 years after publication, is on average higher than individually-authored papers. This suggests that contributing to collaborative projects in psychology will likely increase the number of high-rank journal publications to the resume of researchers. Overall, our findings indicate that large-team collaborations can be rewarding for individual researchers both by enabling early scientific impact and by contributing to stronger publication records.

articles_hidden.title: Borderline personality disorder, a diagnosis that cannot be challenged: If rejecting the diagnosis is a symptom, can the diagnosis ever be wrong? A response to Chazhoor and Younger (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Laurence Cobbaert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Chazhoor and Younger describe borderline personality disorder (BPD) as a diagnostic and management challenge in regional inpatient psychiatry, including patients' reluctance to accept the diagnosis and preference for autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD). This Perspective examines the epistemic assumptions embedded in that framing and their implications for trauma, neurodivergence, gender diversity, sensory distress and iatrogenic harm.
Conclusions: Diagnostic disagreement is not evidence for the diagnosis being disputed. BPD is itself historically and culturally situated, and its application can relocate traumatic, neurodevelopmental, sensory and minority-stress-related distress into a purportedly disordered personality. When dissent, self advocacy or reports of harm are reinterpreted through the same construct, diagnostic reasoning risks becoming recursive and unfalsifiable. I argue for moving beyond BPD towards trauma-informed, neurodiversity-affirming, sensory-informed and epistemically just formulations that remain open to revision.

articles_hidden.title: Attention in model-based cognitive neuroscience: Mechanisms for optimization under constraint
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Ruth Weichart; Ryan Pierce Kirkpatrick; Jared Vance
articles_hidden.abstract: Two major criticisms of attention research are: 1) verbal theories lack the specificity to make falsifiable predictions about how the various mechanisms of attention operate; and 2) the term ``attention’’ is frequently ascribed to conceptually similar phenomena despite dissociable neural underpinnings. The field of model-based cognitive neuroscience is well-positioned to address (1) through mathematical formalization of hypothesized processes, but may perpetuate (2) insofar as similar algorithms and parameters may recur across modeling traditions without necessarily drawing upon a shared neuro-mechanistic basis. This review provides a function-first organization of the algorithms that have been hypothesized to implement or give rise to ``attention'' at various levels of processing: perception, decision-making, and learning. We ground mathematically-formalized processes in the performance-relevant objectives they serve and the processing constraints that limit them. In doing so, we provide a road map of the broader computational-level solutions that ``attention'' mechanisms have been invoked to provide.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Validation of the Mental Health Screening Tool for Children and Adolescents (MHST-CA)
articles_hidden.authors: Diana Vasile; Șerban Andrei Zanfirescu; Ana Cosmoiu; Teodora Georgescu; Marina Badea; Monica Senchiu; Dragos Iliescu; Alina Aldea
articles_hidden.abstract: Existing adolescent mental health screening instruments are predominantly symptom-focused, lack integration of biological, psychological, and social dimensions, and have limited validation evidence in Eastern European populations. This study describes the development and validation of the Mental Health Screening Tool for Children and Adolescents (MHST-CA), a brief self-report instrument grounded in the biopsychosocial model. Item generation drew on 22 focus groups (N > 200) and interviews with 31 specialists. An initial 132-item pool was reduced through exploratory factor analysis in a pilot sample (N = 237, ages 10-20) and confirmatory factor analysis in a validation sample (N = 496, ages 10-20, 58.1% female). For the final 27 items, the hypothesized correlated three-factor model was not supported (CFI = .88), whereas a bifactor model with a general factor and three biopsychosocial facets fit well (CFI = .92, TLI = .91, RMSEA = .06, SRMR = .05, ωH = .88, ECV = .76) and is proposed post hoc as the measurement model. Internal consistency was high (α = .84-.94) and measurement invariance held across gender and age group. The total score correlated with the DASS-Y (r = .82), CPSS (r = .73) and WEMWBS (r = -.69) and identified elevated posttraumatic stress symptoms (AUC = .90). Controlling for age, gender and the DASS-Y, the Biological and Social subscales added ΔR² = .085 in predicting well-being. The MHST-CA offers a brief, culturally grounded screening tool for Romanian adolescents, best interpreted as a total score. Limitations include reliance on self-report and a geographically restricted sample.

articles_hidden.title: Similarity Judgments Reveal the Multidimensional Representations of Naturalistic Faces
articles_hidden.authors: Natalie Peluso; Amanda K Robinson; Tijl Grootswagers; Julie Henry; Jessica Taubert
articles_hidden.abstract: The human face affords a remarkable array of complex social cues, yet our understanding of how it is spontaneously perceived relies almost exclusively on controlled, posed stimuli that suppress the natural variation which makes faces so informative. Here, using a data-driven similarity task with 75 naturalistic face images, we mapped 182,500 perceptual judgments across 365 adults aged 20 to 76. The results indicated that naturalistic face space was hierarchically organized by expressive and demographic cues: smiling faces formed a coherent category that transcended gender and age, whereas non-smiling adult faces stratified along apparent gender. Representational similarity analysis showed that affective dimensions (valence, intensity, energy), emotion category, demographic cues (age and gender), and image-based color each uniquely predicted similarity judgments, while specific personality traits and facial action unit intensity did not. These results demonstrate that highly variable naturalistic faces carry potent combinations of both categorical and dimensional information, advancing a more ecologically valid framework for understanding real-world social perception.

articles_hidden.title: The Power of Narrow Traits (PNT) Framework: How Behavior Accumulates Across Situations into Life Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Michael P. Grosz
articles_hidden.abstract: Broad traits predict consequential life outcomes but are ill-suited to causal inference, whereas single narrow, behaviorally measured traits are more interpretable causally but predict weakly. The space of narrow traits is also so large that choosing among them is challenging. I propose the Power of Narrow Traits (PNT) framework to address both challenges. In a specific person, the causal effect of a narrow trait (e.g., talkativeness) on a specific outcome (e.g., social capital) accumulates across the situations in which the trait can be expressed as a state (e.g., talking) and in which that state influences the outcome, with situations described by their features. In its basic form, four factors multiply at each point of the feature space: (a) how often per year the person encounters such situations, (b) over how many years, (c) how strongly the trait translates into the state there, and (d) how strongly that state causally affects the outcome. These contributions are then summed over the situations the person encounters. The decomposition clarifies when narrow traits should be consequential, which traits to measure for a given outcome, why the same trait level leads to an outcome for some people but not for others, and how interventions can be tailored to each person's trait and situational profile. I formalize the framework, illustrate it with worked examples, relate it to existing theories, and derive six empirical predictions. PNT thus provides a unifying structure for future work on stable individual differences and life outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: llmClassificR: Text Classification with Large Language Models, Network Psychometrics, and Calibrated Uncertainty in R
articles_hidden.authors: Hudson Golino
articles_hidden.abstract: Text classification has become a central measurement problem in psychology and the social sciences, and the arrival of large language models (LLMs) multiplied the number of available strategies, from contextual encoders and embedding services to prompted generative models and, more recently, general-purpose classification models such as Jev, which return probabilities for typed questions about a text. The present paper introduces the R package llmClassificR, which brings these strategies together in a single, consistent interface, and shows how they can be combined with network psychometrics, complexity science, and modern uncertainty quantification. The package implements (a) unsupervised classification of texts with exploratory graph analysis applied to the embeddings of local encoder models, decoder LLMs, and embedding APIs, including a prime-weight encoding that combines the networks estimated from every transformer layer into a single multiplex representation; (b) supervised classification heads on frozen embeddings, evaluated by cross-validation; (c) prompted classification with generative LLMs, with shuffled batching, label validation, strict JSON Schema outputs, ensembles, and self-consistency; (d) retrieval-augmented, automated, and human-guided topic discovery; (e) Jev-based classification with Choice, Noul, and Score questions; (f) do-it-yourself Jev-like classifiers built from label descriptions and local or API embeddings; and (g) calibration, temperature scaling, Platt scaling, selective classification, and conformal prediction sets. The tutorial uses synthetic texts generated by LLMs, descriptions of emotional situations labeled by the people who wrote them (EmpatheticDialogues), and Reddit comments labeled by several raters (GoEmotions), which makes it possible to show how methods that look nearly perfect on synthetic data behave on real text, how the reliability of the labels limits the accuracy that any classifier can demonstrate, and how model uncertainty relates to human disagreement.

articles_hidden.title: Phantom limb behaviour and gaze during obstacle avoidance: obstacle shunning and tolerance after upper-limb amputation
articles_hidden.authors: David Crevillén Hernández; Manfredo Atzori; Steffi Weidt; Emily S. Cross; Gianluca Saetta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Phantom limb sensations persist in most amputees and offer a window into how the body is represented without sensory input from the missing limb. In this state, vision may help resolve conflicts between the perceived body and the physical world. In obstacle tolerance (OBT), the phantom remains present despite overlapping with physical matter; in obstacle shunning (OBS), it retracts or disappears. Whether these experiences extend beyond subjective perception to visual attention during action remains unclear.
We tested whether OBS and OBT are associated with distinct gaze and task-performance patterns during obstacle avoidance. Fifteen individuals with transradial amputation (7 OBS, 8 OBT) and 29 able-bodied controls physically executed or imagined a limb repositioning movement while avoiding an obstacle. We recorded gaze using mobile eye-tracking and quantified obstacle-directed dwell time using automated obstacle segmentation and fixation detection. We analysed trial duration and attention shifts between the obstacle and the limb or environment.
Bayesian mixed-effects models showed that participants with OBT spent less time looking at the obstacle when using the affected rather than the intact limb during motor execution. They were also more likely to make three or fewer attention shifts with the affected-limb, suggesting reduced obstacle monitoring when phantom–object overlap is tolerated. Participants with OBS took longer than controls during both motor execution and motor imagery.
These findings suggest that OBS and OBT are associated with distinct action-related visuospatial strategies. Phantom–object relations appear to extend beyond subjective experience to the visual and temporal organisation of behaviour around physical objects.

articles_hidden.title: Two Decades of Reading Performance at the Alouette Test: Descriptive Data and Dyslexia  Screening Properties in French Primary School Children
articles_hidden.authors: DUCROT; Brice Brossette; Tom Chetrit; Bernard Lété
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: The Alouette test is widely used in France to assess reading performance and screen for dyslexia. Its low semantic predictability text limits contextual compensation and emphasizes word identification. However, its 2005 standardization relied on small grade-level samples, evidence on its screening properties in school-age children remains limited, and temporal changes in performance are poorly documented. 
Methods: We pooled 5,118 Alouette assessment records from typically developing French-speaking children in Grades 1–5, collected across research projects between 2004 and 2025. We examined grade and sex differences and associations with school socioeconomic status. Screening properties were evaluated in 744 children with a prior diagnosis of developmental dyslexia and 744 matched controls. Temporal associations were examined using regression models accounting for grade, sex, and school socioeconomic status, with school-level clustering addressed where appropriate. Sensitivity analyses examined age and school composition, and exploratory models compared gradual trends with change around 2018, when French educational reforms placed renewed emphasis on foundational reading skills and structured phonics. 
Results: Performance improved across grades on all indices except errors, with no substantial sex differences. Associations with school socioeconomic status were stronger in the upper grades. Children with dyslexia performed more poorly on all indices. The areas under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves were .861 for reading accuracy and .902 for reading efficiency. At grade-specific 10th-percentile thresholds, reading efficiency yielded 76.3% sensitivity and 88.6% specificity. Across assessment years, reading efficiency increased by about 0.6% per year on average, whereas accuracy declined slightly, mainly in Grades 1 and 2. Exploratory models favored a difference of approximately 9% in reading efficiency between observations collected before and after 2018 over a single linear trend, although patterns varied across indices.
Conclusions: This study provides extensive descriptive data on Alouette performance and evidence of its potential for dyslexia screening. The proposed thresholds require independent validation before routine clinical use. Retrospective sampling and discontinuous temporal coverage limit generalizability, and the observed post-2018 difference cannot be attributed with certainty to education reforms.

articles_hidden.title: Bonobos and chimpanzees: revisiting the aggression dichotomy
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Maloueki; Bekeli Nseu Mbomba
articles_hidden.abstract: Aggression in the genus Pan (including bonobos and chimpanzees) remains a central puzzle in primatology and anthropology. Traditionally framed as a dichotomy between “peaceful bonobos” and “violent chimpanzees,” recent findings challenge this view by documenting coalitionary aggression, maternal cannibalism, and lethal intergroup encounters in bonobos, alongside evidence that captive chimpanzees and bonobos exhibit comparable aggression levels. These observations highlight the importance of ecological context, demographic composition, and behavioral plasticity in shaping aggression. We propose that species identity is a weaker predictor of aggression in Pan than socioecological, demographic, social, and neuroendocrine context. While captivity offers methodological control, it also introduces confounds such as reduced group size, absence of fission–fusion dynamics, and enforced proximity. Conversely, wild studies reveal the ecological pressures, territorial defense, resource distribution, and interspecies competition that drive variation in aggression. Future research must integrate captive and free‑ranging data through hybrid protocols, quantify ecological and demographic drivers, and explore neuroendocrine mechanisms underlying sex‑specific aggression. An integrative review on Pan aggression will refine our understanding of adaptive strategies, illuminate the evolutionary roots of human social conflict, and advance comparative models of primate behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Testing Group Differences in Network Models using Bayesian Model Selection: A Tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas M B Haslbeck; Mona Klau; Tessa F. Blanken; Maarten Marsman
articles_hidden.abstract: Network models are increasingly used to model multivariate data and many research questions are about whether networks differ across groups. This tutorial provides an accessible introduction to Bayesian model-selection for testing group differences in networks, as implemented in the R package bgms. This approach provides posterior inclusion probabilities and Bayes factors for each group difference, allowing researchers to distinguish evidence for a difference from evidence for equality. We focus the tutorial on group differences in ordinal network models, since the vast majority of data in cross-sectional research are measured on ordinal scales. We explain the model parameters, prior choices, missing-data handling, convergence checks, checks of model fit, and the interpretation of posterior summaries of group differences. The workflow is illustrated with a reproducible comparison of problematic pornography use symptom networks in women and men.

articles_hidden.title: Reinforcement learning processes underlying the onset and maintenance of compulsive ritualistic behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Tal Erdinast; Eran Eldar; Nitzan Shahar
articles_hidden.abstract: Compulsive rituals in OCD present a fundamental puzzle for theories of human learning. How can an action acquire value as a means of preventing harm even though the individual recognizes that the action has little or no causal influence on the feared outcome? We propose that this apparent contradiction can arise from automatic credit assignment, whereby actions that precede favorable outcomes are reinforced even when those actions are known to be causally irrelevant. When harm is anticipated but no adverse outcome occurs, the absence of harm may reinforce the preceding action, allowing an objectively ineffective behavior to acquire harm prevention value. We formalize this account using an actor-critic reinforcement learning model in which actions are performed under fluctuating states of subjective perceived threat. Simulations show that agents possessing such false credit assignment mechanisms develop persistent ritualistic behavior in an objectively uncontrollable environment. We find that ritualistic behavior is especially likely to persist when feared outcomes are rare and highly aversive, making the ritual appear consistently effective in preventing a catastrophe. We further describe the cost-effectiveness of ritualistic behavior, and provide a computational account of how compulsive rituals can emerge as goal-directed attempts to prevent harm, persist despite explicit causal knowledge, and subsequently acquire anxiety-reducing properties. This work may help explain the persistence of compulsive behavior and inform mechanisms through which therapy can reduce it.

articles_hidden.title: Individual Differences and Conflicting Intuitions in Explaining Variance in Philosophical Thought Experiments
articles_hidden.authors: John Protzko; Joshua Knobe
articles_hidden.abstract: When people are asked about philosophical thought experiments, the result is usually that different people give different responses. A question arises as to whether this variance is primarily a matter of differences between different people (between-person variance) or primarily a matter of each individual person giving different answers on different occasions (within-person variance). We disentangle these two sources of variance by administering five different thought experiments to participants and then giving them the same thought experiments again two weeks later. Across the five thought experiments, 66% to 79% of people gave the same answer both times. Using the intraclass correlation, we can compute the proportion of person-variance vs. within-person variance. Across the thought experiments, 25% to 52% of the total variance was between-person variance. Overall, these results indicate that a substantial proportion of the variance in responses to philosophical experiments is due to stable individual differences. Further research can explore which specific individual differences account for the between-subject variance and which specific cognitive processes account for the within-subject variance, but although the present study does not address those questions, it does provide an estimate of the total proportion of variance due to each of these sources.

articles_hidden.title: Information-Seeking Behavior in Mice (Mus musculus) During Visual Discriminations: Evaluating Metacognitive and Alternative Accounts in a Target-Cueing Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Kazuhiro Goto; Yuya Hataji
articles_hidden.abstract: Information-seeking behavior is often interpreted as evidence of metacognitive monitoring, but nonmetacognitive factors may also explain such behavior. We examined this issue in mice using a target-cueing procedure in which an information-seeking response produced a hint indicating the location of the rewarded stimulus. In Experiment 1, mice performed an orientation discrimination. In Experiment 2, the same mice performed a grating discrimination in which grating coarseness varied across trials. During training, some aspects of performance were compatible with a metacognitive account. In Experiment 1, information seeking did not increase reliably as the discrimination became more difficult, although hint use improved accuracy most clearly at smaller orientation differences. In Experiment 2, mice sought information more often at lower grating coarseness, and hint use was associated with the greatest accuracy benefit under those more difficult conditions. However, the critical test results did not support the prediction that information seeking would track the need for additional information. Mice frequently sought information in target-only trials, in which no additional information was required, and showed relatively low rates of information seeking in trials in which the initial display consisted of two identical, and therefore nondiagnostic, stimuli. These findings indicate that information seeking in the present task was multiply determined. The observed pattern was consistent with contributions from competition, reinforcement history, and the behavioral utility of the hint. Although some aspects of training remained compatible with confidence-based control, the critical test conditions showed that information seeking was not governed by confidence monitoring alone.

articles_hidden.title: Illumination and the Emergence of Creative Ideas: A Dual-Route Model
articles_hidden.authors: Carola Salvi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Illumination has occupied a central position in theories of creativity since Wallas identified it
as one of the four phases of the creative process. Although subsequent models have continued
to recognize illumination as the moment at which new ideas emerge into awareness, relatively
little attention has been devoted to the cognitive processes underlying this transition. At the
same time, a parallel literature on insight problem solving has generated extensive evidence
describing the processes that precede and accompany the sudden emergence of new ideas, yet
these findings have rarely been integrated into broader theories of creativity. This chapter brings
together these traditions to reconsider illumination within the broader process of creative idea
generation. Building on classical and contemporary theories of creativity, a Dual-Route Model
of Creative Idea Generation is proposed. In the continuous route, intermediate states remain
accessible to conscious awareness as an idea develops. By contrast, in the discontinuous route,
an idea becomes abruptly available to conscious awareness, following processing that is not fully
accessible to introspection. Behavioral, metacognitive, and neurocognitive evidence relevant to
these different modes of idea emergence is reviewed, alongside their potential relationships with
the quality and subsequent memory of the ideas generated. Finally, the broader implications
of the framework are considered by examining insight as a possible form of model updating,
outlining the main empirical predictions of the Dual-Route Model, and discussing its relevance
to creative problem solving in engineering and design.

articles_hidden.title: What Generalizes in Reliability Generalization?
articles_hidden.authors: Brett Reynolds
articles_hidden.abstract: Zhao and Plonsky's synthesis of task-engagement research uses a distribution of reported reliability coefficients to assess measurement quality and discuss minimum acceptability. Such judgments require more than a position in that distribution. As the authors note, the pooled coefficients don't all summarize the same measurement property, and even comparable coefficients have different consequences for different scientific targets. Using the synthesis as a worked case, this response connects the authors' cautions about coefficient choice to their rationale for a percentile benchmark. Under explicit classical-error models, reliability of .6 leaves a randomized raw mean contrast unbiased but reduces its effective sample size to 60% of the original. An uncorrected slope on a noisy predictor instead converges to 60% of the latent slope. Standardized differences and correlations require further distinctions. These familiar results show why a field percentile alone can't tell a researcher what a planned study can learn. A worked planning example shows how, under the stated model, reliability and sample size together set the precision of an experimental contrast. Reliability syntheses can better support such decisions by displaying comparable coefficients separately and connecting them to uncertainty about specified estimates and predictions.

articles_hidden.title: The Paradox of Modern Love:  Why Romantic Signals Decline in Developed Societies
articles_hidden.authors: Edgar Dubourg; Julien Lie-Panis; Valentin Thouzeau; Coralie Chevallier; Marta Kowal; Piotr Sorokowski; Nicolas Baumard
articles_hidden.abstract: Converging evidence shows that the cultural importance of romantic love has increased dramatically with societal development; it now serves as a primary criterion for choosing partners, a foundation for family formation, and a pervasive theme in cultural production. Yet here we show that this rise does not continue indefinitely: romantic love peaks and then declines at the highest levels of development. This rise-and-fall pattern emerges both cross-nationally (9,474 participants across 45 countries) and diachronically (automatic annotations of 13,409 U.S. movies, 1971–2020). This poses a puzzle: if romantic love sustains long-term pair-bonds, and if safer, more affluent environments make such bonds more viable, why would love decline where it should thrive? We resolve this paradox by proposing that what declines is not love itself, but the need to signal it. Using a formal model and cross-national analyses (N=7,333 and 84,382), we show that when long-term commitment becomes common, overt romantic signaling becomes unnecessary and even counterproductive: the most committed individuals benefit from not signaling, because doing so would reveal that they expected the relationship to need reassurance. In affluent societies, love becomes quieter not because bonds are weaker, but because they are more secure.

articles_hidden.title: When Can Ultra-Short Paired-Comparison Assessment Recover Trait Information? A Simulation and Empirical Illustration
articles_hidden.authors: David Gallardo-Pujol; Laura Viñals-Vilà; Núria Arimany; Elisenda Tarrats Pons
articles_hidden.abstract: Ultra-short comparative assessments reduce respondent burden, but compression also reduces the information available for score recovery. This article evaluates ultra-short graded paired-comparison (GPC) assessment as a design-contingent information-recovery problem. Study 1 examined 324 Monte Carlo data-generating conditions varying construct saturation, stimulus validity, nuisance variance, pair construction, and test length, with three response formats and multiple recovery methods evaluated within each condition. Across 1,000 replications per condition, design factors dominated average format differences. GPC responses recovered benchmark information under favorable conditions, retained more information than binary paired choices, and deteriorated when target signal was weak, nuisance variance was systematic, or pair construction was contaminated. Reliability could increase while benchmark recovery declined. Study 2 applied this framework to three-pair image-GPC versions of the STAI-6 and SABAS. The STAI implementation showed strong benchmark recovery across constrained ordinal scoring, keyed and component scores, cross-validated prediction, and descriptive multitrait-multimethod checks. The SABAS implementation showed weak recovery across the same diagnostics. The findings support a conservative conclusion: ultra-short GPC assessment can work, but only when the construct, stimuli, pair construction, response format, length, and scoring method jointly preserve enough target-relevant information.

articles_hidden.title: Genetic and Environmental Connections Shared between Transmissible Liability to Substance Use Disorder and Substance Use Initiation
articles_hidden.authors: Hermine H M J L Maes; levent kirisci; William G. Iacono; Diana R. Samek; Judy Silberg; Emily B. Zimmerman; Chao-Yi Lo; Mei-Hsin Su; Medhin Tsegaye; Maria Fatima Ali
articles_hidden.abstract: In the absence of face-valid indicators, particularly in children, liability to substance use/addiction requires quantification. The Transmissible Liability Index (TLI) was developed for this purpose by employing a high-risk design and item response theory and quantifies this liability in childhood, before substance exposure. Because the TLI places liability to substance use disorder on a common scale, it can also facilitate harmonization across datasets collected from different populations. This study extends prior research by examining genetic and environmental contributions to TLI and its relationship with liability to the initiation of licit and illicit substance use. The study utilizes data of TLI, and substance use tracked from age 11 to age 25 from longitudinal twin studies in Virginia and Minnesota.  Results showed that TLI is highly heritable and that substance use initiation (SUI) reflected a mixture of genetic and shared environmental influences varying across substance classes, consistent with the principle that initiation is more environmentally sensitive than progression. The genetic correlations between childhood TLI and lifetime SUI are consistently stronger than the environmental correlations and support a developmental interpretation in which early heritable liability manifests in SUI and, further downstream, in disorder. In addition to confirming TLI’s high heritability, predictive validity, and utility for dataset harmonization, it supports the feasibility of identifying high- and average-resistance samples, to be used for selecting specific indicators of resistance to substance use/addiction.

articles_hidden.title: A cultural evolutionary approach to organising academic meetings
articles_hidden.authors: Friederike Hillemann; Elena Miu; Ilaria Pretelli; Ivan Kroupin; Sheina Lew-Levy
articles_hidden.abstract: Academic meetings are central to sharing and discussing research, and key events for networking and community-building. Their design shapes interaction patterns and knowledge flow. Drawing on insights from cultural evolution, we outline how meetings can be structured to reduce disciplinary echo chambers and to foster inclusive, interdisciplinary exchange and cumulative knowledge building. Cultural evolution offers tools for understanding how meeting formats shape information transmission, learning, and the persistence of ideas, and how design choices at all stages of the cultural evolutionary process act as selection pressures. For example, meetings aimed at generating new ideas benefit from broad exposure to diverse perspectives and flexible interaction patterns, whereas meetings focused on consolidating knowledge rely on repeated interaction for refinement and alignment. While few researchers organise large-scale conferences, many take on the role of organising symposia, workshops, or lab retreats, where design matters just as much. This guide offers theory-informed, practical principles to support organisers of meetings across diverse formats and constraints.

articles_hidden.title: Can a Brief Online Intervention Raise Adolescents’ STEM Expectancy and Values? A Four-Arm Randomized Trial of Goal Setting and Role Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Jane E Boyle; Geetanjali Basarkod; Johnmarshall Reeve; Emily Q Rosenzweig; Nicholas Francesco Graziani; Jiesi Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents’ expectancies and subjective task value beliefs for STEM decline across secondary school, yet few trials have compared different intervention components for enhancing these beliefs within the same trial. This four-arm randomized trial, framed by situated expectancy-value theory, compared brief online interventions focused around goal setting, role modeling, their combination, and an active control. Participants were 855 Year 9 students (401 female, 454 male; M age = 14.68) across six Australian schools (3 urban, 3 rural). Outcomes were expectancy, intrinsic value, utility value, and perceived cost for STEM overall and, in exploratory analyses, for biology, chemistry, and physics. Compared to the control condition, the goal-setting-only condition produced higher post-intervention expectancy (Δ = 0.17, q = .034) and intrinsic value (Δ = 0.18, q = .034) but not utility value. Role modeling alone produced no significant benefit after statistical correction. The combined condition raised expectancy but also perceived cost. No gender interaction was significant. In rural (compared to urban) schools, exploratory analyses showed that, relative to the active control, goal setting alone raised utility value (Δ = 0.46, q < .001) and role modeling alone raised expectancy (Δ = 0.11, q < .001). Exploratory subject-specific analyses showed similar goal-setting gains. Results suggest that a brief, structured online goal-setting sequence can raise adolescents’ immediate STEM expectancy and intrinsic value, warranting longer-term follow-up.

articles_hidden.title: Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change
articles_hidden.authors: Douglas G. Lee; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles_hidden.abstract: Choice-induced preference change refers to the tendency for value estimates to differ after a choice relative to before it. Although this phenomenon is robust, the process that generates it remains debated. In this work, we reanalyzed pooled data from two previous studies to identify empirical signatures to serve as benchmarks for candidate process accounts of choice-induced preference change. We focused on three factors that are especially informative for theory: choice difficulty, deliberation time, and the attribute structure of the options. First, we reproduced the well-established finding that the spreading of alternatives is greater for more difficult choices. Second, we showed that its relationship with response time remains after controlling for difficulty, indicating that the relationship with deliberation time is not reducible to initial value difference alone. Third, we found that preference change depends not only on overall value difference but also on how the options differ in terms of their attributes, with stronger effects for choices laden with tradeoffs than for cases of simple dominance. Together, these results indicate that choice-induced preference change is tied to deliberation itself rather than to a post hoc or artifactual revision of fixed values. The findings are compatible with both value-refinement and coherence-based reasoning accounts in some respects, but they also constrain both by showing that preference change depends jointly on difficulty, deliberation time, and attribute structure.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Consequences of Challenge: the Degree to which Spoken Word Recognition Changes in Response to Difficulty has Independent Relevance
articles_hidden.authors: John Baltazar Muegge; Bob McMurray
articles_hidden.abstract: Listeners must often recognize words in challenging listening conditions like background noise. The cognitive mechanisms of spoken word recognition offer a potential locus for adaptation to such contexts. Indeed, research has found that the millisecond-by-millisecond dynamics of word recognition in challenging conditions differ lawfully along a small number of dimensions. However, comparatively little is known about the factors that impact the nature of an individual listener’s response to challenge. Here we ask if this response is stable across time and challenge type, if it is constrained by the idiosyncrasies of how listeners recognize words in quiet, and if these patterns of processing predict performance in real-world outcome measures. We tested listeners in a Visual World Paradigm with two different types of challenging listening across two days. We then leveraged a principal component analysis to extract underlying dimensions of variance across these conditions. Using this approach, we found that the dynamics of word recognition in challenge are predicted by their dynamics in typical speech, that these dynamics are stable across days and different types of challenge, and that the magnitude with which listeners change recognition predicts their performance in tests of speech-in-noise comprehension.

articles_hidden.title: Breaking the Stasis in the Polyvagal Controversy: Two Category Errors, a Missing Variable, and a Measured Boundary
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriel Kram; Heather MacDuffie
articles_hidden.abstract: For twenty years, the dispute over Polyvagal Theory (PVT) has turned on whether the profound bradycardia attributed to dorsal vagal shutdown occurs in ordinary human freezing and dissociation. The 2026 Grossman–Porges exchange sharpened that dispute without resolving it. We argue that it cannot be resolved as framed, because neither position specifies the variable that would adjudicate it: the pervading neurochemistry under which a recruited circuit operates. PVT made the required observation once, in 2001, when it paired oxytocin-conditioned calm immobilization with vasopressin-conditioned immobilized fear at identical dorsal vagal anatomy. The observation was never generalized, because the neurochemical model PVT inherits retains a two-pole structure in which the endogenous opioids have no position. We propose a three-variable model in which neuroception selects the circuitry recruited and modulatory chemistry determines what that circuitry produces. As a falsifiable hypothesis, severable from the model, we propose that the cardiac and respiratory signature of life-threat immobilization requires endogenous µ-opioid activity, and that naloxone administered during confirmed shutdown should reverse bradycardia and restore respiration on the timescale of the drug’s onset. Independently of the model, electron-microscopic fiber counts of human vagal tissue show that the supradiaphragmatic/subdiaphragmatic discontinuity is confined to the myelinated population, placing that partition on direct measurement rather than comparative inference. Because escapability rather than phylogenetic age selects the state, PVT’s clinical claims do not depend on its evolutionary reconstruction. The observations of both parties describe physiologically distinct conditions, and the model, drawn from Autonomics, converts a twenty-year standoff into experimentally decidable predictions.

articles_hidden.title: Does Outcome Utility Bias the Mental Simulations of Risky Events?
articles_hidden.authors: Yun-Xiao Li; Johanna Falben; Lucas Castillo; Jake Spicer; Jian-Qiao Zhu; Stella Qian; Nick Chater; Adam N Sanborn
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the utility of an outcome influence people's assessment of risk and uncertainty? Prominent theories propose that people rely on mental simulation to evaluate probabilities and risky events, yet prior empirical findings is mixed as to whether and how utility biases this process. Across four experiments (total N=206, with Experiment 4 pre-registered), we tested this question using a random generation paradigm, in which participants mentally simulated gamble outcomes and said them out loud. Then we compared these responses with probability judgments and predictions. While we identified individual differences, the majority of participants exhibited neutrality, with no systematic impact of utility on their sampling distributions. Nevertheless, an optimism subgroup emerged, with a larger proportion of optimistic participants when the monetary context was more salient. Additionally, outcome utilities have similar effects on probability judgments, predictions, and random generation tasks, consistent with the proposal that these tasks are related to each other and may all rely on mental simulation. These findings indicate that utility does not uniformly distort mental simulation, but can do so for a stable subgroup under particular motivational contexts, and they motivate cognitive models that capture both unbiased and optimistic forms of mental sampling.

articles_hidden.title: The Emergent Structure of Memory Phenomenology Depends on Whether Memories Are More Episodic or Semantic
articles_hidden.authors: Tabatha Blaney-Gale; Jordan Poppenk
articles_hidden.abstract: Phenomenological characteristics are central to theoretical distinctions among modern memory constructs. The scene construction framework proposes that episodic remembering involves the construction of coherent scenes, such that the structure of phenomenology may reflect the engagement of the hippocampus and related regions during recall. However, most phenomenology research relies on instruments with content and scoring schemes that embed theoretical assumptions into their measurements. Here, we explored whether phenomenological characteristics emerge from self-reported memory experiences as anticipated by episodic memory theory. We solicited memories from a large online sample, following each response with a novel questionnaire designed to evaluate the phenomenology of individual memories. We used folded bottom-up factor analyses to examine and validate the global latent factor structure of participants’ memory experiences. Consistent with Tulving’s declarative memory framework, our analyses produced five stable dimensions: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, mental time travel, relational memory, and semantic memory. In order, these dimensions reflect multi-modal perceptual reexperiencing, personal meaning, sense of reliving, detailed spatiotemporal context, and conscious use of semantic knowledge during recall. The semantic memory dimension has no clear predecessor, suggesting the strategic use of general knowledge during recall is a distinct and previously uncharacterized aspect of remembering. This factor structure generalized across memories elicited by recent and remote episodic prompts. However, distinct versions of mental time travel and relational memory emerged in response to the semantic prompt, suggesting these dimensions of memory are context-sensitive rather than fixed. While our findings validate the link between episodic memory and its theorized phenomenological elements, they also invite broader investigation of how phenomenology may vary across different classes of memory.

articles_hidden.title: When Creativity Goes Rogue:  Semantic Organization in Conspiracy Thinkers and Politically Extreme Individuals
articles_hidden.authors: Dina Mohamed; Steven Verheyen
articles_hidden.abstract: This study addresses a gap in previous research by examining how semantic memory organization relates to conspiracy endorsement and political extremism. A total of N = 98 participants completed the Generic Conspiracist Beliefs (GCB) scale and an animal verbal fluency task (M_age= 27.88, 〖SD〗_age = 11.45; 59.18% female; 69.39% European). Of these, n = 96 also completed a self-placement political extremism item. Participants were grouped according to their levels of conspiracy thinking (high or low) and political extremity (moderate or extreme). We hypothesized that 1) political extremism would predict conspiracy thinking, 2) that individuals high in conspiracy thinking would exhibit flexible semantic networks, similar to those found in creative individuals, and that 3) politically extreme participants would exhibit similar semantic patterns to participants high in conspiracy thinking. Semantic networks were constructed from verbal fluency responses, and we compared the respective group networks’ clustering coefficient (CC), average shortest path length (ASPL), modularity (Q), and small-world-ness (S). Results showed that political extremism negatively predicted conspiracy thinking. High conspiracists exhibited more flexible semantic networks, consistent with patterns previously observed in creative individuals. Politically extreme individuals showed efficient global connectivity but lacked local associative clustering. These findings suggest that semantic memory structure is meaningfully linked to conspiratorial and ideological beliefs. Longitudinal research is needed to clarify the causal direction of these associations.

articles_hidden.title: Who with OCD gets referred? A 10-point deprivation gap in English primary care records
articles_hidden.authors: Himanshu Tyagi; Mustafa Sarang; Chrissy Jayarajah; Rajeev Kolluri; Nick Sireau; Mark Paramlall
articles_hidden.abstract:
BACKGROUND: 

Psychological treatment and SSRIs are both first-line options for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), but whether people in deprived areas receive the same kind of care is unknown. NICE has published tables from English primary care records (CPRD Aurum) for two possibly overlapping cohorts: 20,253 people diagnosed within three years and 7,271 newly diagnosed.

AIMS: 

To establish whether deprivation is associated with which care is recorded, mental health referral or SSRI prescribing, in adults and children.

METHOD: 

We verified NICE's 1,171 values, rebuilt counts from rounded percentages, repeated every test over all admissible counts with multiplicity, clustering and missing-data sensitivity analyses, and compared findings with national prescribing, NHS Talking Therapies data and 25 published studies.

RESULTS: 

Among newly diagnosed adults, 42% in the most deprived fifth had a mental health referral recorded, against 52% in the least, while SSRI prescribing barely differed (61% against 62%). In the three-year cohort, referral was 41% against 48% and SSRI prescribing higher in the most deprived fifth (54% against 49%). The two outcomes' slope indices differed by 17.0 percentage points (three-year cohort; Holm-adjusted P < 0.001) and 15.5 (newly diagnosed; Holm-adjusted P = 0.041; Bonferroni 0.082). NICE's comorbidity-adjusted estimates were similar. In newly diagnosed children, exploratory analyses showed referral of 46% against 54% (odds ratio 0.70 to 0.75), and lower SSRI prescribing in Asian than White children (0.60 to 0.65). In national NHS Talking Therapies data, OCD formed a smaller share of anxiety referrals in areas whose referrals came more from deprived neighbourhoods (Spearman's rho −0.48), unlike generalised anxiety disorder.

CONCLUSIONS: 

In what are, to our knowledge, England's only national primary care data on OCD and BDD, deprived areas had less recorded mental health referral but no less SSRI prescribing: equal prescribing should not be read as equal care. Child differences need confirmation; linked records could show whether the gap is in treatment received.

articles_hidden.title: On the size of the model selection problem in a conjoint measurement experiment
articles_hidden.authors: Kenneth Knoblauch; Frederic Devinck
articles_hidden.abstract: We examine how the number of models respecting marginality in model selection using Maximum Likelihood Conjoint Measurement (MLCM) varies with the number of dimensions tested and explain the logic for determining this number.  The results are related to Dedekind numbers, which increase super-exponentially, and, thus, suggest a limit to the number of dimensions that can be practically tested using the MLCM paradigm.

articles_hidden.title: Voluntary Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Mindful Scale (VCHIMMS)
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin Sheldrake; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: The Voluntary Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Mindful Scale (VCHIMMS) is a reformulation of the Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (Sheldrake & Dienes, 2026) as instructions for mindful, voluntary behaviour, as opposed to imaginative suggestions for automatic, involuntary behaviour.

articles_hidden.title: Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (CHIMSS)
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin Sheldrake; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract:
The Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (CHIMSS) is a novel set of imaginative suggestions that each demand the utilisation of phenomenological control. This scale consists of three suggestions of each type: motor suggestions for arm levitation, hands coming together, and head nodding; challenge suggestions for hands stuck together, fingers stuck together, and arm immobilisation; imagery involvement suggestions for a beach scene, an animal-identification scene, and a future scene; and hallucination suggestions for a mosquito, two tastes, and hearing a song playing automatically. The scale notably excludes suggestions for amnesia, post-hypnotic behaviour, and visual hallucinations. It also includes three alternative imagery involvement suggestions that can be used in place of the existing ones or in addition: a meadow scene, a woods scene, and a scene involving identification with a celestial being or superhero.
The introduction script and suggestions were modified from the Phenomenological Control Scale (Lush et al., 2021). The imagery involvement suggestions were modelled after the Imagery Involvement/Dissociation suggestion in the Elkins Hypnotizability Scale (Elkins, 2013, pp. 99–124).

articles_hidden.title: When Does Reputation Help the Future? Audience Presence and Identity Disclosure in Intergenerational Resource Dilemmas
articles_hidden.authors: Mingyuan Sheng; Ye Niu; Xiaoli Ling
articles_hidden.abstract: Many environmental problems, from climate change to resource depletion, are intergenerational dilemmas: the present generation bears conservation costs, whereas the benefits go to future generations, who can neither observe nor reciprocate. Reputation reliably sustains cooperation among contemporaries, but whether it works across generations remains unclear. In two experiments using an intergenerational goods game, we examined how the audience of disclosure and the type of information disclosed affect contributions to a resource passed from one generation to the next, and whether social value orientation (SVO) moderates these effects. In Experiment 1, disclosing to the next generation what participants had contributed increased the rate of sustained generations but did not reliably increase individual contributions or narrow the gap between prosocial and proself individuals. In Experiment 2, disclosing the same information to present peers increased both individual contributions and the rate of sustained generations. Adding names and faces was tentatively associated with a further increase in contributions, although this condition was recruited in a separate wave. These gains came mainly from proself individuals, whose contributions no longer differed from those of prosocial individuals when names and faces were disclosed. The findings suggest that disclosure promotes intergenerational cooperation chiefly when it reaches an audience present at the time of decision, and that identifiability matters most for those least motivated to cooperate. Making conservation visible to future generations may not be enough; it may also need to be visible to someone now, suggesting a potentially low-cost approach to promoting environmental cooperation.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Battlefield: A Cross-Sectional Study of War-Related Stressors and Mental Health in Four Central European Countries
articles_hidden.authors: Piotr Długosz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Prolonged armed conflicts may affect mental health beyond the battlefield through indirect, war-related stressors. However, evidence on populations outside the immediate conflict zone remains limited. This study assessed psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms and examined their associations with coping strategies among adults in four Central European countries more than two and a half years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in October 2024 with 2,962 participants from Poland (n = 728), Czechia (n = 743), Slovakia (n = 742), and Hungary (n = 749). Participants were recruited from opt-in online research panels using stratified quota sampling based on sociodemographic characteristics. Psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were measured using the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10), the Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7), and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), respectively. Between-country differences were examined using one-way analysis of variance, and associated factors were assessed using country-specific linear regression models.
Poland had the highest mean scores for psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms (K10: F(3, 2,958) = 12.61; GAD-7: F(3, 2,958) = 9.40; PHQ-9: F(3, 2,958) = 7.10; all p < 0.001). Czechia had the lowest mean scores for distress and anxiety. Mean depressive symptom scores were lower in Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary than in Poland, with no significant differences among the three countries. The average item-level selection rate was higher for problem-focused than for emotion-focused strategies in all four countries. Younger age, lower perceived quality of life, and greater use of emotion-focused coping were associated with higher symptom scores. Problem-focused coping was associated with lower symptom scores only in Poland.
Mental health symptom scores differed across the four countries, as did some associations between coping strategies and mental health. The findings support continued monitoring and attention to groups reporting poorer outcomes. Given the cross-sectional design, the observed associations do not establish causal effects.
Keywords: Transboundary mental health; armed conflict; psychological distress; anxiety; depression; coping strategies; Russia–Ukraine war; Central Europe.

articles_hidden.title: Depression-Anxiety Comorbidity Across Sex During COVID-19: An Evaluation of Partial Invariance with Invariance Partial Pruning
articles_hidden.authors: Xinkai Du; Asle Hoffart; Sacha Epskamp; Helga Ask; Ragnar Nesvåg; Sverre Urnes Johnson
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression and anxiety co-occur so frequently that comorbidity is more prevalent than the occurrence of either in isolation. The conventional latent-variable perspective offers limited insight into comorbidity because its inherent causal assumptions overlook causal relations among observable symptoms that are meaningful for explaining comorbidity. At the same time, comorbidity studies based on the network perspective have largely relied on cross-sectional data, which cannot capture the dynamic nature of mental disorders, or on two-wave panel data, which does not separate between- and within-variance and biases the estimation of dynamic processes. Therefore, we present a dynamic network analysis of depression-anxiety comorbidity with the panel graphical vector autoregressive model, using invariance partial pruning to consider possible network structural differences between biological sex. Results revealed the central role of fear in predicting depressive moods and anhedonia as a possible explanation of comorbidity. Anxiety symptoms temporally preceded depression symptoms. In the contemporaneous networks, nervousness and fear were connected to depressive mood. Furthermore, worry and rumination were more associated with depression, whereas beliefs about the uncontrollability of worry and threat monitoring were more associated with anxiety. No sex difference was discovered.

articles_hidden.title: Co-constructed Emotion: A Collective Predictive Coding Theory of Interoception and Social Symbol Sharing
articles_hidden.authors: Takato Horii; Chie Hieida; Yuri Terasawa; Ohira Hideki; Tadahiro Taniguchi
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotion is both a psychological phenomenon rooted in physiological fluctuations and a socially constructed phenomenon shaped by language and culture. However, traditional psychological constructivism has remained confined to individual brain processes, while social constructivism has lacked a bottom-up computational mechanism explaining how language and culture emerge from bodily emotional substrates and dynamically evolve. To bridge this theoretical gap, this paper proposes the Theory of Co-constructed Emotion (TCoE) via Collective Predictive Coding (CPC), a framework coupling physiological regulation with social symbol sharing within a single active inference formulation. We extend the conventional CPC model by explicitly incorporating interoception---which is indispensable for modeling emotion from a physiological perspective---into each agent's generative model, alongside exteroception and internal and external representations. In TCoE, the co-construction of emotion is described as a dual inference process: an internal loop of allostasis regulating individual bodily states, and a social loop of communication sharing emotional concepts with others. These loops mutually minimize prediction errors mediated by shared symbols (emotion words). We argue that this theoretical framework 1) aligns with psychological findings on emotional contagion and concept formation, 2) enables constructive verification in multi-agent robotic systems, and 3) provides a computational redefinition of psychiatric conditions such as alexithymia as a disconnection between interoception and social symbols. Thus, we offer a novel computational foundation for emotion research that unifies individual embodiment and social symbol systems.

articles_hidden.title: On Great Ape Personality Structure: Problems in Minkov (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Weiss
articles_hidden.abstract: A recent paper (Minkov, 2026) claimed that great ape personality is not well-described by the five personality dimensions found in humans, those being Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness to Experience, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. To support this claim, the author analyzed personality factor structures obtained in studies of great apes in which personality was assessed using rating scales. The analyses tested for ‘configural invariance’ by computing the percentage of traits that loaded on the same factor as in humans in chimpanzees, orangutans, mountain gorillas, and bonobos, and the percentage of traits that loaded on the same factor across four studies of chimpanzees. The paper also reviewed the evidence for Conscientiousness in chimpanzees, including by citing the results of studies that used other ratings scales, and concluded that this factor’s evidentiary basis was weak. The paper concluded by proposing an alternative approach to studying personality in great apes. This commentary exposes fundamental problems with the article. First, I show that the paper’s author mischaracterized the research program of comparative psychologists who study personality. Second, I review the evidence the paper uses to support its claim that there is little evidence for configural invariance, highlighting problems and errors in the analyses and reporting of results. Third, I review the evidence presented against the presence of Conscientiousness in chimpanzees and find it problematic. Finally, I demonstrate that the literature review lacks due care. I conclude by dispelling a misunderstanding about comparative research on personality and reaffirm the importance and promise of pluralism in the study of the phenomenon.

articles_hidden.title: An orthographic advantage in spoken word recognition: Behavioral and ERP evidence from cross- and within-modal priming in Korean
articles_hidden.authors: Joonwoo Kim; Solbin Lee; Kichun Nam
articles_hidden.abstract: Spoken word recognition may benefit from orthographic information even when spelling differs from surface pronunciation. Korean Hangul preserves spelling across regular phonological changes, allowing us to compare primes matching a target’s written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U). We report two EEG experiments with independent participant groups, using primed auditory lexical decision on the same 120 disyllabic Korean targets, with within-modal auditory primes (Experiment 1) and cross-modal visual primes (Experiment 2). In both experiments, O primes shortened response latencies and improved accuracy relative to U primes, and produced greater behavioral benefits than P primes. The O–P latency advantage was larger with visual than auditory primes. Phonological latency priming was modest with auditory primes and was not established with visual primes, whereas evidence favored no between-experiment difference in orthographic latency priming. Orthographic relatedness was associated with more positive centro-parietal amplitudes in the N400 window (350–550 ms) in both experiments, without clear evidence of a between-experiment difference. Following visual primes, it also increased fronto-central positivity in the 250–350 ms window, more than following auditory primes. The predicted P200 enhancement was not reliably established. The behavioral O–P advantage was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference. The findings suggest that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation and support a role for orthographic relations in spoken word recognition.

articles_hidden.title: NICE’s 2026 Consultation Draft Guideline for OCD and BDD (GID-NG10435): A Critical Appraisal with Secondary Analysis of NICE’s Published Data
articles_hidden.authors: Himanshu Tyagi; Mark Paramlall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. In September 2026 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) opened consultation on the first batch of its update to the 2005 guideline for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (GID-NG10435). The draft replaces stepped care with matched care and reviews first-line treatment.

Methods. We appraised the draft and its supporting documents against six questions informed by selected AGREE II domains, analysing NICE’s published effect estimates, sample sizes, sensitivity analyses and economic results descriptively; every value was checked against its source document. Comparison guidelines were identified by a documented search.

Results. The adult OCD review included 82 randomised controlled trials and the BDD review 13 studies. The committee cited small samples and wide credible intervals when it did not recommend metacognitive therapy (52 participants) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR; 59 participants). Self-administered cognitive behavioural therapy with therapist support, the second adult option, rests on 61 participants, with a wider credible interval than EMDR’s, and was recommended on other documented grounds.
